title: Three Hardware Wallets That Scream Bitcoin. Twenty Backups That Don't.
description: 2-of-3 multisig vs. 2-of-20 singlesig. The economics of Bitcoin self-custody, privacy, and why we've made a simple problem so complicated.

blocks.html: 2-of-3 multisig vs. 2-of-20 singlesig. The economics of Bitcoin self-custody, privacy, and why we've made a simple problem so complicated.
At some point Bitcoin self-custody turned into a hardware shopping hobby.
Buy a hardware wallet. Write down twenty-four words. Hide them somewhere.
Worried about losing the device? Buy another one. Worried about trusting one manufacturer? Buy a third, preferably from someone else.
Now configure 2-of-3 multisig, back up three seeds, preserve your wallet descriptors, keep the firmware updated, and figure out which software will coordinate the whole thing.
Congratulations. You've bought three little electronic billboards advertising that you probably own Bitcoin.
I prefer an ordinary laptop running Bitcoin Core, an encrypted file, and a passphrase.
I can make twenty copies of my recovery material, distribute them across different locations, and need only one encrypted file and one corresponding passphrase to recover my wallet.
Each component can be stored without revealing that it has anything to do with Bitcoin.

If I want another independent component, I add another encryption layer. If I want more redundancy, I make more copies. If I want part of my recovery process located several hours away, I arrange that too.
This is an approach to self-custody built around a simple economic question: how much does it cost me to defend my Bitcoin, and how much would an attacker have to spend to compromise it?
Multisig has a privacy problem built into its purpose

blocks.alt: Multisig distributes signing authority, along with information about the wallet being secured.
blocks.caption: Multisig distributes signing authority, along with information about the wallet being secured.

blocks.html: Multisig is designed to distribute spending authority.
In a 2-of-3 wallet, two signatures are required to spend. In 3-of-5, three. In 5-of-10, five.
That makes perfect sense when several independent people need to approve transactions.
But why has it become the default recommendation for someone who simply wants redundant backups of their own Bitcoin?
Multisig participants are supposed to verify what they're signing. They need to understand the spending policy and examine the transactions they're asked to authorize.
In a typical multisig arrangement, signers share a wallet descriptor containing the public keys and rules needed to reconstruct the wallet.
Someone with that complete descriptor can reconstruct the wallet's addresses and examine its transaction history and balances on the blockchain.
That's useful when independent participants are responsible for authorizing spending.
It becomes awkward when privacy is one of your main objectives.
Suppose I give a friend one of my three hardware wallets for safekeeping, along with the recovery information normally needed to restore that signer and its multisig configuration.
My friend can recognize the device. The descriptor identifies the spending policy and potentially reveals the balance being protected.
They don't have enough signatures to steal the Bitcoin, but they may now know exactly what they're helping me secure.

Multisig signers can be configured to reveal less information, and the backup material can be encrypted. Yet the normal arrangement is built around multiple participants independently verifying a common spending policy.
Keeping every participant ignorant of that policy rather defeats the purpose.
Trying to turn a distributed authorization system into an arrangement of anonymous recovery components is an awkward exercise.
The individual signer still needs private, redundant backups.
And the obvious way to protect those backups is encryption.
Which is where I'd rather begin.
My 2-of-20 Bitcoin Core singlesig

blocks.alt: Ten encrypted files. Ten passphrase copies. Any matching pair can recover the entire wallet.
blocks.caption: Ten encrypted files. Ten passphrase copies. Any matching pair can recover the entire wallet.

blocks.html: I create a wallet using Bitcoin Core on an ordinary offline computer running minimal Debian Stable.
I back up the wallet and encrypt the complete backup with GPG, using a randomly generated passphrase.
Now I have two components.
The first is an encrypted file.
Someone who finds the encrypted file has no idea what's inside. It could be anything. There's simply no way to tell from the encrypted contents.
I can store copies on USB drives, optical media, in the cloud, in bank deposit boxes, or give them to people for safekeeping. Nobody holding a copy needs to know what it contains.
The second component is the passphrase.
I use KeePassXC to generate five random English words and write them on paper.
Someone finds those five words. What are they? Who knows? They're just five random words on a piece of paper. Nothing recognizable, certainly nothing that suggests Bitcoin.
I make ten copies, put each one in an envelope, and store them in different locations or give them to people for safekeeping.
Now I have ten encrypted wallet files and ten passphrase copies, all stored separately.
Twenty backup artifacts.
To recover my wallet, I need any one encrypted file and any one matching passphrase.
I can lose nine copies from either group and still recover everything.
And none of those twenty copies needs a Bitcoin label.
The resulting recovery process is remarkably simple.
Find one encrypted file. Obtain its passphrase. Decrypt it. Restore the wallet in Bitcoin Core.
I can explain that to anyone who has used a computer.
Three friends holding backups shouldn't become a spending committee

blocks.alt: Three friends holding the same password have one credential. Two friends holding multisig signers can have your Bitcoin.
blocks.caption: Three friends holding the same password have one credential. Two friends holding multisig signers can have your Bitcoin.

blocks.html: Suppose I have three friends I trust.
I'd like each of them to safeguard one copy of my recovery material.
With my approach, I can give each friend an identical copy of the same five-word passphrase.
None of them needs to know what the words are for.
Now suppose all three friends meet, open their envelopes and compare the contents.
What have they accomplished?
They've discovered that they're holding three copies of the same five words.
Putting those copies together gives them nothing they didn't already have individually.
They still don't possess the encrypted wallet file.
Three identical passwords don't magically become three different keys.
Now imagine I've given these friends three fully usable signers from the same 2-of-3 multisig wallet.
The trust assumptions are completely different.
Any two friends who cooperate can authorize a transaction without me.
If they have the wallet descriptor, they can also inspect the balance and the spending policy.
Suddenly, storing my recovery material has turned into a question about relationships between several people.
Do they know each other? Do they know that they're holding separate signers for the same wallet? Can they communicate? What happens if their incentives change?
I've introduced collusion risk into an arrangement whose original purpose was simply protecting backups from loss.
With layered encryption, I can give ten people ten copies of the same credential without turning them into a signing committee.
They cannot gain additional spending authority merely by combining identical copies.
My friends can help me preserve access to the wallet without becoming participants in its spending policy.
I'd rather trust someone to safeguard an envelope than make that person one of the people authorized to spend my Bitcoin.
Want another component several hours away? Add another encryption layer.

blocks.alt: Add another encryption layer, and put an essential recovery credential a few hours out of reach.
blocks.caption: Add another encryption layer, and put an essential recovery credential a few hours out of reach.

blocks.html: Now suppose physical coercion is part of my threat model.
Someone might confront me and demand that I unlock my Bitcoin.
I'd like to arrange things so that I genuinely cannot assemble the wallet immediately.
Perhaps one essential recovery component should be several hours away.
I don't need another hardware wallet for that.
I take my existing GPG-encrypted backup and encrypt it again with GPG, using a second independent passphrase.
Now recovery requires three components: the twice-encrypted file and both passphrases.
I can keep the encrypted file and first passphrase nearby while storing every copy of the second passphrase several hours away.
I deliberately don't memorize that second passphrase or keep it on my phone. My working signer is also secured so it doesn't provide an immediate alternative way to spend.
I now have a genuine logistical barrier between myself and full wallet access.
Or I can reverse the arrangement.
I can keep the passphrases nearby and store the encrypted file remotely.
I can distribute all three components across different cities or countries.
I decide how many components are required and how far apart they must be.
Now suppose I make ten copies of each.
Thirty backup artifacts, with one copy from each group required for recovery.
Bitcoin Core itself also supports wallet encryption, which can protect the private keys inside the wallet with another independent passphrase.
And I can add more external encryption layers if my circumstances justify them.
Think of a vault with several doors.
Every door has its own key. I can make redundant copies of those keys and place them wherever I choose.
The model scales surprisingly far.
At its simplest, it's one encrypted file and one passphrase, perhaps with a few copies stored nearby.
A family might prefer three independent components distributed among several locations.
At the opposite extreme, imagine fifty consecutive encryption layers, each with a different credential.
You'd have fifty passphrases and one final encrypted file.
Make ten copies of each component and you have 510 backup artifacts.
You could distribute them across six inhabited continents, with recovery requiring one copy from every group and fifty successive decryptions.
I'd hate to organize that recovery drill, but the underlying architecture hasn't changed.
The number of required components, the redundancy of those components, and the geographical separation between them are all under my control.
I don't need to change the Bitcoin spending policy every time I decide to add another door to the vault.
The economics of brute force: a five-word passphrase can mean hundreds of billions of dollars

blocks.alt: One extra random word multiplies the attacker's search space by 7,776. Generating it takes seconds.
blocks.caption: One extra random word multiplies the attacker's search space by 7,776. Generating it takes seconds.

blocks.html: Security has an economic price.
KeePassXC can generate random passphrases using the EFF wordlist, containing 7,776 possible words.
Four randomly selected words give approximately 3.66 quadrillion combinations.
Five give roughly 28.4 quintillion.
Six give approximately 221 sextillion.
Every additional random word multiplies the number of possible combinations by 7,776.
Let's translate that into dollars.
Published Hashcat benchmarks show an NVIDIA RTX 4090 processing roughly 30,000 to 33,000 guesses per second against Bitcoin Core's native wallet encryption.
For a comparison, we can also model a GPG AES-256 file using SHA-512 and a high S2K count, around 65 million bytes, at an illustrative 15,000 guesses per second per GPU.
Suppose an attacker rents 10,000 RTX 4090 GPUs at $0.89 per GPU-hour.
Here's the time and rental cost required to exhaust the complete search space under those assumptions.

Random wordsBitcoin CoreGPG
4141 days / $30 million282 days / $60 million
53,003 years / $234 billion6,006 years / $469 billion
623.4 million years / $1.82 quadrillion46.7 million years / $3.64 quadrillion

These are full-search calculations. A successful search takes roughly half that effort on average. Actual costs depend on the encryption settings and available hardware; the GPG column is a modeled high-iteration configuration.
But consider the relationship between the cost of attack and defense.
I can generate a five-word passphrase in seconds.
In this model, the computing resources needed to exhaust its search space cost hundreds of billions of dollars.
And an attacker finding my encrypted backup doesn't even know that the passphrase has five words.
Perhaps it has six. Perhaps eight.

They don't know whether the file contains Bitcoin. They don't know its value. They don't know whether decrypting it would simply reveal another encrypted file protected by another independent passphrase.
Even a technically capable attacker has to decide whether the potential reward justifies the cost.
My cost of adding another random word is negligible. The search space becomes 7,776 times larger.
Another encryption layer costs me practically nothing to create. An attacker who breaks the first layer may still have more work to do.
And making ten redundant copies of a credential costs almost nothing compared with the amount of redundancy I gain.
This is how I want to think about Bitcoin security.
I know exactly what I'm protecting and how the recovery components fit together.
The attacker starts with very little information.
The resulting economic asymmetry is much more interesting to me than the number of expensive signing devices I can collect.
The hardware-wallet industry has become a honeypot industry

blocks.alt: The secure element is only one part of the attack surface. The supply chain and customer database are targets too.
blocks.caption: The secure element is only one part of the attack surface. The supply chain and customer database are targets too.

blocks.html: The hardware-wallet industry has spent years explaining why specialized devices are the safest place for Bitcoin private keys.
Since July 2026, we've had an impressive demonstration of how many different things can go wrong.

Coldcard suffered a seed-generation flaw connected to approximately $116 million in stolen Bitcoin. A firmware defect weakened the randomness of certain wallets, allowing attackers to reconstruct private keys without physically accessing the devices.
BitBox patched severe firmware vulnerabilities.

Trezor had customer information exposed through its shipping provider, affecting 80,689 people. Another breach involving its email provider exposed 347,149 newsletter contacts and enabled targeted phishing.
SafePal disclosed a vulnerability affecting 39,798 customer records.
Then came the physical implants.

Ledger confirmed that genuine devices sold through the CryptoBilis reseller had been modified with unauthorized hardware designed to capture recovery words during setup and transmit them over a cellular connection.
The secure element didn't have to fail. Attackers modified the surrounding hardware before it reached the customer.
On October 30, Trezor warned customers about a credible report of a similar implant in a Safe 5 sold through the same reseller. The reported device had not yet been physically examined by Trezor.

Keystone suffered a breach that exposed customer information and its WebAuth authentication key. The compromise created the possibility of counterfeit devices passing the manufacturer's own authenticity checks. Keystone announced plans to destroy 18,835 devices from the affected inventory.
Foundation, the manufacturer of the Passport wallet, experienced a compromise of backend infrastructure that enabled phishing messages to appear as though they came from official company domains.
Different incidents, different attack methods.
Some affected private-key security. Others exposed customers, authentication systems or distribution channels.
But consider the information being accumulated around these products.
Names, home addresses, email addresses, phone numbers and purchase histories can identify people who have bought specialized equipment for securing valuable assets.
A person who has purchased a Bitcoin hardware wallet has already told someone what type of asset they probably care about protecting.
And the resulting customer databases can become targets in their own right.
Apparently, after spending hundreds of dollars on devices designed to protect private keys, the customer now needs to worry about the security of the manufacturer's shipping provider.
I would prefer not to create that dependency.
The biggest honeypots are custodians and exchanges

blocks.alt: Billions concentrated in one place give attackers billions of reasons to find a way in.
blocks.caption: Billions concentrated in one place give attackers billions of reasons to find a way in.

blocks.html: The same economic logic applies to centralized custodians.
Whenever someone points out a potential difficulty with self-custody, the industry has another familiar suggestion: let a professional hold your Bitcoin.
But professional custodians can be compromised too.
Mt. Gox collapsed in 2014 after the loss of hundreds of thousands of Bitcoin.
Coincheck lost approximately $530 million in 2018.
In February 2025, attackers stole around $1.5 billion from Bybit. The FBI attributed the theft to North Korea.
The compromise involved the signing workflow around a large pool of assets, illustrating how attackers can exploit the software and people surrounding an authorization system.
Then came the October 2026 Binance incident.

Binance reported approximately $6.3 billion in unauthorized withdrawals. Its preliminary investigation pointed to a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop that may have allowed attackers to access internal infrastructure and submit unauthorized transactions.
The exchange reported no evidence that wallet private keys had leaked. About $3 billion of the affected assets had been frozen by October 30.
An attacker may not need to extract private keys if they can compromise the systems that instruct legitimate signing infrastructure to authorize transactions.
And centralized custody isn't limited to exchanges.
On September 6, attackers exploited a validation bug in Elements, the software underlying Blockstream's Liquid Network.
They created approximately 4,000 unbacked L-BTC and used the network's peg-out mechanism to withdraw roughly 4,000 actual BTC from the federation reserves.
Around 3,400 BTC was subsequently returned.

Blockstream also manufactures the Jade hardware wallet. The Liquid exploit wasn't a Jade vulnerability, but it demonstrated how a concentrated pool of Bitcoin can become vulnerable through other software and operational dependencies in the surrounding ecosystem.
None of these attacks required defeating Bitcoin's underlying cryptography.
The attackers identified economically attractive targets and found exploitable paths through their infrastructure.
Large custodians can invest enormous amounts in security. They can employ specialists, develop sophisticated procedures and maintain expensive systems.
They also hold enormous amounts of value.
An attacker may find it economically reasonable to spend millions of dollars developing an attack against an institution controlling billions.
And cryptocurrency theft has already created well-funded attackers with the resources to invest in future operations.
This is a contest between the cost of defense and the expected reward from attack.
A large centralized honeypot creates a large potential reward.
An individual or family operating a private Bitcoin Core wallet presents a different economic calculation.
They can adopt the same underlying security principles used by professional operators, without concentrating billions of dollars on one operational platform.
Generic computers. Linux. Bitcoin Core. Offline signing. Encrypted backups. Carefully separated credentials.
The same engineering disciplines, adapted to an individual's circumstances.
There's no need to make the system more complicated than the risk requires.
Your privacy can leak before anyone touches your keys

blocks.alt: Your private keys can remain secure while third-party wallet servers collect clues about your Bitcoin.
blocks.caption: Your private keys can remain secure while third-party wallet servers collect clues about your Bitcoin.

blocks.html: Hardware-wallet software introduces another set of privacy questions.
A surprising number of people use wallets through coordinator applications connected to public servers or third-party infrastructure.
Those services may learn which wallet addresses or transactions the user is interested in. Depending on the setup, they can also observe IP addresses and related network information.
If those records are compromised, attackers may be able to correlate Bitcoin activity with information about the person using the software.
Now combine that with a leaked hardware-wallet customer database containing names, emails and shipping addresses.
Or with information obtained from an internet provider or another compromised service.
The attacker can begin assembling a picture of who owns what, where they live and which Bitcoin transactions may belong to them.
These are exactly the kinds of information leaks that make targeted attacks economically attractive.
And now consider what AI does to the cost of exploiting those records.
Cybersecurity researchers are already documenting increasingly automated attacks that use AI agents for reconnaissance, phishing and credential theft.
An attacker can use stolen customer information to create individualized messages, impersonate support personnel, and run many social-engineering conversations at once.
The old phishing email written in broken English is becoming a historical curiosity.
When attackers can automate research, personalization and impersonation, a leaked list of cryptocurrency customers becomes considerably more useful.
I'd rather avoid being on that list.
Running my own Bitcoin Core node also removes the need to send my wallet's address queries to a public third-party wallet server.
My node validates transactions independently and keeps the wallet information under my control.
The objective is straightforward: minimize how much information about my Bitcoin reaches people who don't need it.
Bitcoin Core has a different economic security advantage

blocks.alt: Bitcoin Core has accumulated public scrutiny since 2009, backed by an economy that depends on its reliability.
blocks.caption: Bitcoin Core has accumulated public scrutiny since 2009, backed by an economy that depends on its reliability.

blocks.html: Bitcoin Core occupies a very different place in the Bitcoin economy from an individual hardware-wallet vendor.
It's one of the principal implementations of Bitcoin's validation software.
Exchanges, miners, infrastructure operators, businesses and individual Bitcoiners all depend directly or indirectly on software that correctly enforces the network's rules.
Bitcoin Core's history goes back to 2009. Its code has accumulated years of public review, testing, bug fixes and real-world use.
Anyone can inspect it, build it, test it and propose improvements.
And the economic incentive to identify vulnerabilities is enormous.
Consider what happened in October 2026.
Project Loupe, an AI-assisted security research initiative at Block-backed Spiral, discovered a vulnerability in Bitcoin Core's network handling.
The bug could allow a malicious connected peer to crash certain Windows, macOS and BSD nodes by exhausting their memory.
Linux nodes were unaffected.
It was a node-availability problem rather than a way to steal wallet funds.
Gregory Sanders verified the finding. Antoine Poinsot prepared the fix, which was merged on October 26. Bitcoin Core 31.2 and 32.1 shipped with the patch the following day.
Four days after the automated scan discovered the problem, patched releases were already available.
That tells me something about the economic resources supporting Bitcoin Core.
An organization funds automated security research. Independent developers validate findings. Maintainers review and repair the code. The improvements become available to everyone.
The benefit extends well beyond the customers of a particular manufacturer.
Bitcoin Core has an unusually mature codebase, an enormous accumulated history of public scrutiny, and many participants with direct financial reasons to want it working correctly.
And anyone can use the finished software for free.
On an ordinary computer.
Your grandmother doesn't need to become a full-time phishing analyst

blocks.alt: If Grandma can save a file, copy it, and use a password, she can learn the foundations of Bitcoin self-custody.
blocks.caption: If Grandma can save a file, copy it, and use a password, she can learn the foundations of Bitcoin self-custody.

blocks.html: Bitcoin Core 32.1 arrived on October 27 with performance improvements that can make blockchain synchronization faster.
It also added something I've wanted in the graphical interface for years: Export Watch-Only Wallet.

blocks.alt: Article illustration

blocks.html: That makes my preferred two-computer setup much easier.
One ordinary computer runs Bitcoin Core online. It independently verifies the blockchain, tracks the wallet and prepares transactions.
Another computer stays offline and holds the private keys.
You create the wallet on the offline computer, then export a watch-only copy through Bitcoin Core's graphical interface and transfer it to your online node.
The online wallet can see your addresses and balance but cannot sign transactions.
When you want to send Bitcoin, the online node prepares a PSBT, a Partially Signed Bitcoin Transaction.
You transfer that transaction to the offline computer using removable media, inspect it, sign it, and return the signed transaction for broadcast.
The normal wallet export, restoration and PSBT workflow can now be handled through Bitcoin Core's graphical interface without manually typing descriptor-import commands.
And the backup?
It's the same encrypted wallet file we've been discussing.
Think about your grandmother.

If she's ever created a Word document, saved a file, copied photographs onto a USB drive or used a password, she already understands the basic operations behind Bitcoin Core wallet creation and backup.
Create Wallet is conceptually like creating a document.
Backup Wallet is like saving a copy of an important file.
Encrypting the backup means protecting a file with a password.
Making redundant backups means copying that encrypted file.
Layered encryption means protecting it again with another independent password.
Computers have supported these ideas for decades.
She doesn't need to begin by learning BIP39 derivation paths, extended public keys, wallet fingerprints, multisig descriptors, firmware compatibility and transaction coordinators.
Nor do I particularly want her spending the next decade years monitoring hardware-wallet security announcements and wondering whether the latest urgent email is genuine.
Imagine she's bought a hardware wallet, and her name, email, phone number and home address later appear in a leaked customer database.

Now consider a future attacker equipped with increasingly capable AI agents that can research victims, impersonate support employees, write convincing personal messages and automate phishing conversations.
Why should she have to deal with that additional exposure simply because she wanted to save in Bitcoin?
And if her shipping address becomes associated with a valuable Bitcoin holding, the concern extends beyond phishing.
The $5 wrench attack becomes more plausible when an attacker knows where a potential target lives.
Trezor itself warned that its 2026 shipping-data breach could increase physical security risks for affected customers.
This is why I care so much about privacy as part of the original custody design.

My grandmother shouldn't have to become a security analyst who constantly evaluates fake firmware alerts, AI-generated support calls, suspicious recovery instructions and possible supply-chain compromises.
She should be able to understand her wallet, operate it on an ordinary computer, and keep private backup components in places of her choosing.
Using generic hardware doesn't place her on a hardware-wallet manufacturer's customer list.
Running her own Bitcoin Core node avoids handing wallet queries to public wallet servers.
Keeping encrypted files and independent passphrases gives her recovery material that doesn't identify the asset being protected.
Those choices remove unnecessary sources of information that attackers would otherwise be happy to exploit.
It seems like a much better starting point than asking her to buy three Bitcoin-branded devices and spend the rest of her life watching for security advisories.
Use Bitcoin spending policies for the problems they were designed to solve

blocks.alt: Multisig decides who can spend. Timelocks can restrict when. Encryption protects the recovery credentials.
blocks.caption: Multisig decides who can spend. Timelocks can restrict when. Encryption protects the recovery credentials.

blocks.html: Bitcoin already supports more sophisticated spending rules when they're needed.
Multisig can determine which combination of signers must authorize a transaction.
Timelocks can determine when a particular spending path becomes available.
Taproot and Miniscript provide ways to describe and combine more advanced conditions, with support available in Bitcoin Core.
These tools are useful when the circumstances actually require them.
A company treasury may need several directors to approve spending.
An inheritance arrangement may benefit from a recovery path that becomes available after a specified block height or time.
An institution may have multiple authorization procedures for different circumstances.
Those are genuine reasons to design a more sophisticated Bitcoin spending policy.
But most individuals don't need to begin there.
Their immediate problems are much more ordinary.
How do I prevent someone from stealing my Bitcoin?
How do I avoid losing access to it?
How do I make the backups private?
How do I recover everything years later?
Bitcoin Core, encrypted backups, independent credentials and redundancy provide a straightforward foundation.
We can add more elaborate spending policies when we can explain exactly what problem they're supposed to solve.
Understanding that distinction makes the entire custody problem easier to reason about.
Bitcoin custody in 2140

blocks.alt: Imagine millions of private, independent Bitcoin vaults instead of a handful of enormous honeypots.
blocks.caption: Imagine millions of private, independent Bitcoin vaults instead of a handful of enormous honeypots.

blocks.html: Bitcoin has completed four of the thirty-three halvings that will eventually bring the block subsidy to zero.
The fourth occurred in 2024. The final subsidy reduction is expected around 2140.
We're still early in Bitcoin's monetization, and our custody practices are still evolving.
I wonder what the landscape might look like by the time the last satoshi has been mined.
I can imagine a world with far more sovereign individuals, families and businesses holding their own Bitcoin.

Professional custody will probably continue to serve people who want it. But I'd rather see a broad market of smaller, specialized custodians than a handful of enormous institutions controlling most of the supply.
Some services might specialize in storing encrypted backup components without ever receiving complete spending authority.
Others might provide recovery administration, inheritance services or geographically separated storage.
They could apply mature security practices without concentrating every customer's funds inside one giant operational honeypot.
And individuals could use the same fundamental methods at home.
We already know how to encrypt files, separate credentials, maintain redundant backups and perform recovery drills.
Decades of computer security have given us these techniques.
Bitcoin Core provides the wallet and signing software.
Linux provides a mature operating system.
Generic computers provide replaceable hardware.
GPG and other established tools provide encryption.
KeePassXC generates independent random passphrases.
And regular recovery drills confirm that the system remains recoverable. I prefer a complete restoration test on another trusted machine at least once a year.
The same model can serve a beginner with one encrypted backup and one passphrase, or a family with several independently protected components stored across multiple locations.
A larger institution can scale the architecture further and introduce additional signing authorities where its governance requires them.
The essential building blocks remain understandable.
That's what I'd like people to learn first.
Bitcoin self-custody is entirely achievable without turning your life into a hardware-wallet compatibility project.
We don't have to start with the industry's favorite collection of devices, seed phrases and fashionable multisig configurations.
We can begin with security principles that were well understood long before Bitcoin existed.
A generic computer. Linux. Bitcoin Core.
Encryption, independent credentials, redundant backups and regular recovery tests.
The software has been here since the beginning of Bitcoin. The underlying cybersecurity concepts have been around much longer.
Perhaps the next major improvement in self-custody won't come from another signing gadget, a new proprietary recovery scheme or another influencer explaining which three devices you should buy.
Perhaps we'll simply return to the fundamentals.
Make Bitcoin expensive to attack and cheap to defend.
That's a rather better objective than seeing how many hardware wallets we can fit into a backup policy.

title: Hardware Wallets Are an Economic Security Failure
description: Why Bitcoin-specific supply chains and concentrated rewards change the economics of attacking hardware wallets.

hero.alt: Hardware Wallets Are an Economic Security Failure — Cover illustration

headings.text: 1. The Ledger attack is just the beginning
2. Imagine $100 billion sitting behind a product category
3. Even Apple can't keep its supply chain sealed
4. Trezor is not the escape hatch
5. Multi-vendor multisig, or multiple nightmares?
6. The solution is boring. And that's exactly why it works.
7. The hardware wallet industrial complex
8. Stop treating the symptom
Practical context

blocks.html: The latest Ledger supply-chain attack isn't the problem. The entire hardware wallet industry is.
Following the latest Ledger supply-chain attack, I keep seeing the same advice from Bitcoin influencers:
"Don't buy from resellers."
"Buy directly from the manufacturer."
"Switch to Trezor."
"Use multi-vendor multisig."
And I'm wondering how many more disasters it will take before people recognize that hardware wallets themselves are the problem.
Not Ledger. Not Trezor. Not Coldcard.
The entire category.
Because almost everyone is missing the most important part of the threat model:
The economics of targeted attacks.
And once you understand those economics, the entire hardware wallet security model starts looking very different.
1. The Ledger attack is just the beginning

blocks.alt: Hardware Wallets Are an Economic Security Failure — 1. The Ledger attack is just the beginning illustration
blocks.caption: A compromised reseller is only one link in the chain. The bigger rewards may lie much further upstream.

blocks.html: In October 2026, Ledger began investigating substantial cryptocurrency losses associated with devices purchased through CryptoBilis, an authorized reseller in Southeast Asia. (Ledger update)
On-chain investigators estimated suspected losses exceeding $86 million. (Bitquery investigation)
Ledger subsequently confirmed that at least one affected device contained an unauthorized hardware implant. (Investigation and scope)
The investigation is still establishing the full scope of what happened.
Naturally, the conversation immediately turned to reseller security, tamper-evident packaging, and which manufacturer customers should trust instead.
But there's something fundamentally wrong with that conversation.
Why assume a reseller is as deep as a supply-chain attack can go?
A reseller is only one point in a much longer chain.
There's the component manufacturer.
The chip supplier.
The assembly factory.
The firmware developer.
The quality-control process.
The packaging facility.
The logistics company.
The distributor.
The retailer.
Every stage involves people, procedures, organizations, and opportunities for compromise.
And every one of those opportunities has a price.
The Ledger incident demonstrates what can happen when an attacker reaches one part of that chain.
But what happens when the potential reward becomes large enough to justify going further upstream?
What happens when compromising someone at the factory becomes more profitable than compromising a reseller?
Or when an attacker can influence a component before it reaches the manufacturer?
Or when manipulating a single manufacturing process could affect thousands of devices?
The supply chain doesn't magically become secure because an attacker has to move one or two steps deeper into it.
Those additional steps simply introduce additional costs.
And costs are precisely what financial incentives can overcome.
Which brings us to the much bigger problem.
2. Imagine $100 billion sitting behind a product category

blocks.alt: Hardware Wallets Are an Economic Security Failure — 2. Imagine $100 billion sitting behind a product category illustration
blocks.caption: When the prize is a bearer asset, even a tiny fraction of the total value can justify an extraordinarily expensive attack.

blocks.html: Let's do a simple thought experiment.
Imagine that hardware wallets from a particular manufacturer eventually secure $100 billion worth of Bitcoin.
One hundred billion dollars.
An attacker who manages to steal just 0.1% of that value walks away with:
$100 million.
Now ask yourself a question.
How much would somebody rationally spend to gain access to that money?
$1 million?
$10 million?
Would it be worth recruiting an employee?
Compromising a supplier?
Developing a sophisticated hardware implant?
Spending years researching the manufacturing process?
Of course the answer depends on the probability of success. But that's exactly how attackers calculate these things.
Expected payoff = probability of success × potential reward − cost of attack.
And in the case of Bitcoin, the potential reward can be extraordinary.
We're not talking about stealing customer information that somebody might eventually buy.
We're not talking about industrial secrets that might provide a competitive advantage.
We're talking about private keys controlling bearer assets.
If you obtain the keys and can spend the funds, you're dealing directly with the money itself.
The incentive is immediate and enormously powerful.
Now consider what happens as Bitcoin adoption grows.
A manufacturer secures more Bitcoin.
Its customer base grows.
Its devices become more widely used.
And the potential reward from compromising that manufacturer's ecosystem grows with it.
The security budget of the manufacturer can grow too.
But the attacker doesn't have to defeat the manufacturer's entire security budget.
The attacker only has to find one sufficiently profitable weakness somewhere in the extended system.
A security procedure that is economically effective against a $100,000 attacker may not withstand the attention of a $10 million attacker.
A supply chain that was relatively uninteresting when its devices secured a few million dollars becomes an entirely different proposition when those same devices collectively protect billions.
This is the fundamental contradiction in the hardware wallet business model.
The more successful a hardware wallet manufacturer becomes, the more financially attractive its ecosystem becomes as a target.
Growth doesn't solve the economic problem.
It can amplify it.
3. Even Apple can't keep its supply chain sealed

blocks.alt: Hardware Wallets Are an Economic Security Failure — 3. Even Apple can't keep its supply chain sealed illustration
blocks.caption: If Apple can't eliminate supply-chain leaks, imagine the challenge when the reward isn't a product design, but Bitcoin itself.

blocks.html: Consider Apple.
One of the world's wealthiest technology companies.
A company famous for keeping unreleased products secret until its carefully orchestrated launch events.
Apple has enormous financial resources, sophisticated supplier agreements, dedicated security teams, and decades of experience managing some of the most complex manufacturing operations on Earth.
Yet information still escapes.

In June 2026, Reuters reported that a breach involving Apple's manufacturing partner Tata Electronics exposed confidential information about the upcoming iPhone 18 Pro, including detailed component and supplier information. (Reuters, June 29)
Think about that.
Apple spends extraordinary resources protecting its unreleased products and manufacturing secrets.
And still, information from inside its extended manufacturing ecosystem finds its way into unauthorized hands.
This was a data breach, not a hardware implant. But it illustrates something crucial about supply-chain security.
Even enormous organizations cannot completely control every person, system, and company involved in producing their devices.
Now think about the relative economic incentives.
What's the potential reward for obtaining an unreleased iPhone design?
Perhaps valuable industrial information, a competitive advantage, or media attention.
Now compare that with gaining access to Bitcoin private keys controlling $100 million.
The difference is staggering.
If an attacker is willing to compromise a supply chain for industrial secrets, what happens when the reward is direct access to bearer assets?

And if Apple, with its extraordinary resources, cannot eliminate unauthorized access throughout its extended supplier ecosystem, why should we assume a much smaller hardware wallet manufacturer can guarantee that nobody has tampered with its products?
Security is not simply a question of how much the manufacturer cares. It's a question of whether its defenses remain economically effective against the incentives facing its attackers.
And hardware wallets create exceptionally attractive incentives.
4. Trezor is not the escape hatch

blocks.alt: Hardware Wallets Are an Economic Security Failure — 4. Trezor is not the escape hatch illustration
blocks.caption: Switching manufacturers doesn't eliminate the economic incentive to attack. It simply moves the target.

blocks.html: This is where the usual advice becomes especially absurd.
Ledger has a problem?
Buy Trezor.
Trezor has a problem?
Buy Coldcard.
Coldcard has a problem?
Buy something else.
And every time, the solution conveniently involves buying another specialized Bitcoin device.
But imagine millions of Bitcoiners abandoning Ledger and migrating to Trezor.
What happens to the amount of Bitcoin potentially secured by Trezor devices?
It increases.
What happens to the potential reward from compromising the Trezor ecosystem?
It increases too.
Changing brands doesn't eliminate the underlying economic incentives.
It merely redirects them.
And let's look at what happened over the past few months.

In July 2026, Coldcard disclosed a critical failure in its seed-generation entropy mechanism, affecting firmware released over several years. Weakly generated seeds were exploited, resulting in substantial Bitcoin thefts. (Coinkite security status)

In August, Trezor disclosed a breach involving shipping provider ShipMonk, exposing customers' names, contact information, and shipping addresses. The incident was later found to affect roughly 81,000 customers in total. (Trezor disclosure)

In September, Trezor disclosed another incident, this time involving its email provider Brevo. Attackers exported 347,149 marketing email addresses and used compromised email infrastructure to distribute phishing messages. (Trezor disclosure)
BitBox was affected by a breach of the same email provider, exposing subscriber addresses and enabling fraudulent messages. (BitBox disclosure)
Then, in October, came the Ledger reseller incident and the confirmed unauthorized hardware implant.
Different companies.
Different attack vectors.
Different failures.
Some compromised customer information. Others affected wallet security directly. Some involved the devices themselves. Others involved external service providers.
And that's the point.
A hardware wallet isn't merely a piece of hardware. It's an entire commercial ecosystem.
It's manufacturing, firmware, distribution, logistics, customer databases, support systems, websites, marketing infrastructure, and the people running all of them.
Some of these services are needed to produce the devices; others come with the business that sells them.
And together they create an identifiable concentration of people likely to own Bitcoin.
When attackers obtain a Trezor customer database, they don't have to wonder whether those people might have Bitcoin.
The association is already made.
When attackers compromise a hardware wallet supply chain, they don't have to wonder whether the manufactured device might eventually be used for valuable cryptographic operations.
That is precisely what it is designed for.
Hardware wallets advertise their own economic importance to attackers.
And the more successful the category becomes, the more valuable that targeting information becomes.
5. Multi-vendor multisig, or multiple nightmares?

blocks.alt: Hardware Wallets Are an Economic Security Failure — 5. Multi-vendor multisig, or multiple nightmares? illustration
blocks.caption: Three different logos. Three different supply chains. The same underlying economic targeting problem.

blocks.html: This brings me to perhaps the most frustrating advice of all.
"Just use multi-vendor multisig."
Seriously?
Let's understand what we're actually talking about.
A 2-of-3 multisig requires two independent signing keys to authorize a transaction.
That's a legitimate and extremely useful security property.
If one signer is compromised, the attacker still doesn't have enough keys to spend.
But where does that security property come from?
From Bitcoin.
Not from Ledger.
Not from Trezor.
Not from Coldcard.
Multisig is a Bitcoin authorization model, not a hardware wallet shopping strategy.
Using several vendors can reduce dependence on one manufacturer's specific failure modes. But it does not eliminate the supply-chain risks associated with specialized Bitcoin signing devices.
You still have several identifiable hardware wallet manufacturers.
Several manufacturing ecosystems.
Several firmware implementations.
Several distribution channels.
Several sets of operational assumptions.
And now you have to evaluate, maintain, update, and recover a more complicated system.
You're diversifying manufacturers while remaining entirely within the same economically attractive product category.
That's not the same thing as escaping the underlying targeting problem.
The important question isn't whether three different vendors have three different logos.
It's whether the actual failure domains are sufficiently independent and whether the added complexity improves the entire custody system.
And if you genuinely need a 2-of-3 multisig, there's a very simple question nobody seems interested in asking:
Why do the three signers need to be purpose-built hardware wallets at all?
Why not three independent generic computers?
Three separately maintained environments?
Three signers running Bitcoin Core?
Nothing in Bitcoin's multisig model requires hardware wallets.
The industry has turned what should be a discussion about threshold authorization and independent failure domains into yet another product recommendation.
And somehow we're supposed to believe that purchasing three different specialized black boxes is the pinnacle of security engineering.
One targeted manufacturing ecosystem is already a nightmare.
Three targeted manufacturing ecosystems are multiple nightmares.
You can preserve the cryptographic benefit of multisig without accepting the entire hardware wallet industry's manufacturing assumptions.
So why voluntarily bring those assumptions into your system?
6. The solution is boring. And that's exactly why it works.

blocks.alt: Hardware Wallets Are an Economic Security Failure — 6. The solution is boring. And that's exactly why it works. illustration
blocks.caption: Generic hardware doesn't advertise that it secures Bitcoin. Minimal Linux and Bitcoin Core keep the setup simple and under your control.

blocks.html: Here's the solution.
Stop buying manufactured black boxes whose entire commercial identity tells attackers they are designed to secure Bitcoin private keys.
Use generic hardware.
An ordinary computer.
A used ThinkPad.
A generic desktop PC.
A machine originally built for an enormous, heterogeneous market of people doing entirely different things.
Some of those computers are used for accounting.
Some for writing documents.
Some for software development.
Some for watching movies.
Some for browsing the internet.
And an extremely small fraction might eventually become dedicated offline Bitcoin signers.
Now consider the difference from an attacker's perspective.
If you're compromising the supply chain of a hardware wallet manufacturer, you know exactly what kind of users you're targeting.
People who have purchased specialized devices to secure cryptocurrency.
But when you're looking at the supply chain of generic computers, you're dealing with millions of machines used for countless unrelated purposes.
There's no reliable relationship between a generic computer's make or model and the amount of Bitcoin it might secure.
The market is vastly larger, more heterogeneous, and less informative about the financial value behind any individual device.
That's a fundamentally different economic proposition.
Consider the attacker's expected return on every additional dollar spent developing an exploit.

Why spend enormous resources compromising a broad, generic computing supply chain when a much more concentrated population of Bitcoin holders voluntarily buys devices advertised specifically for that purpose?
Attackers can target generic computers too.
But targeting ordinary hardware as a class is not the same economic problem as targeting specialized devices purchased disproportionately by Bitcoin holders.
The economic attractiveness of a target is determined not only by what it protects, but also by how easily an attacker can identify and reach that value.
Hardware wallets make that identification easier.
Generic hardware makes it less obvious.
And once you choose generic hardware, the next step is to dedicate it exclusively to Bitcoin operations.
Install a clean operating system.
I prefer Debian Stable.
Remove unnecessary software, services, and functionality.
Disconnect the signer from the network permanently.
Create and secure the wallet using Bitcoin Core.
Use a separate online computer running Bitcoin Core to track the blockchain, prepare transactions, and broadcast completed transactions.
Transfer unsigned transactions to the offline signer as PSBTs.
Verify and sign offline.
Return the signed transaction to the online computer for broadcast.
Maintain independently recoverable encrypted backups, protect them with a genuinely strong passphrase, and regularly test recovery.
Generic hardware. Minimal Linux. Bitcoin Core.
No specialized manufacturer required.
No hardware wallet vendor-specific recovery ecosystem.
No dependence on proprietary signing firmware.
No need to purchase your security from a company whose products are explicitly marketed as containers for Bitcoin private keys.
And Bitcoin Core brings something else to the table.
A long history of public scrutiny.
An extraordinarily important role in Bitcoin's infrastructure.
Extensive real-world use.
An open-source codebase that has been studied, tested, attacked, corrected, and improved for many years.
For me, that's a much more compelling software foundation than continually adding specialized custody products and their unique assumptions.
Less novelty.
Fewer unnecessary dependencies.
More control.
More transparency.
And a very different economic attack surface.
7. The hardware wallet industrial complex

blocks.alt: Hardware Wallets Are an Economic Security Failure — 7. The hardware wallet industrial complex illustration
blocks.caption: There's no affiliate commission for installing Debian. No referral code for Bitcoin Core. Follow the incentives.

blocks.html: Of course, you won't hear much about this from the average hardware wallet influencer.
There's no affiliate commission when someone repurposes an old computer.
No referral code for installing Debian.
No new hardware product launch for recommending Bitcoin Core.
No manufacturer-sponsored conference appearance for explaining how to build a minimal offline signing environment.
The hardware wallet industry has developed an entire marketing ecosystem around its products.
Manufacturers.
Affiliates.
Influencers.
Sponsorships.
Conference partnerships.
Product reviews.
Discount codes.
Endless comparisons between devices that all supposedly solve the same problem.
And every new security incident creates another opportunity to recommend a different product.
Something goes wrong with Ledger?
Here's my Trezor affiliate link.
Something goes wrong with Trezor?
Here's a Coldcard discount code.
Worried about the entire situation?
Great. Buy three different devices and call it multi-vendor multisig.
The solution is always more hardware wallets.
That's a remarkable business model.
It's worth asking how much of the advice comes from independently evaluated threat models and how much is simply a repetition of industry conventions reinforced by commercial incentives.
You don't need to assume every influencer is consciously dishonest to recognize the problem.
Financial incentives influence what gets discussed.
Professional relationships influence which assumptions get challenged.
And social incentives influence which opinions are considered acceptable within a particular industry.

If your income, audience, conference invitations, and professional relationships are tied to the hardware wallet ecosystem, challenging the entire category is unlikely to be professionally convenient.
But ordinary Bitcoin holders don't owe the hardware wallet industry anything.
They don't owe manufacturers recurring purchases.
They don't owe influencers affiliate commissions.
They don't owe anybody the acceptance of a particular custody architecture just because it has become fashionable.
Bitcoin security should be an engineering discipline, not a consumer electronics subscription model.
The questions worth asking are simple.
What exactly am I protecting against?
What assumptions does this device introduce?
What would a sophisticated attacker be willing to spend to compromise it?
How concentrated is the reward?
What dependencies can I eliminate?
And can I build the same security properties without relying on a specialized manufacturer?
Those are first-principles questions.
Everything else risks becoming cargo-cult security theater.
8. Stop treating the symptom

blocks.alt: Hardware Wallets Are an Economic Security Failure — 8. Stop treating the symptom illustration
blocks.caption: Stop shopping for security. Start engineering it. Generic hardware. Minimal Linux. Bitcoin Core.

blocks.html: The latest Ledger incident is not a reason to buy a Trezor.
The Coldcard entropy failure was not a reason to buy a Ledger.
The Trezor supply-chain and service-provider incidents are not a reason to buy whichever device happens to be fashionable next.
These events should force us to reconsider the underlying security model.
The problem isn't simply that one manufacturer failed.
Or that one reseller was compromised.
Or that one firmware implementation contained a catastrophic bug.
Or that one logistics provider exposed customer data.
The problem is the enormous economic incentive created by an industry that manufactures identifiable devices whose entire purpose is to secure valuable bearer assets.
And this problem becomes more important, not less, as the amount of Bitcoin secured by those devices grows.
We've spent years arguing about which hardware wallet is best.
Which secure element is best.
Which vendor has the best reputation.
Which device has the most impressive security certification.
Which combination of manufacturers produces the most reassuring multisig setup.
All while largely ignoring the simplest question:
Why are we voluntarily concentrating Bitcoin custody inside recognizable, specialized manufacturing ecosystems in the first place?
The entire premise deserves to be challenged.
Bitcoin doesn't require a hardware wallet manufacturer.
Bitcoin doesn't require branded signing devices.
Bitcoin doesn't require proprietary firmware.
Bitcoin doesn't require security to arrive in an expensive little box.
It requires valid cryptographic keys, correctly implemented signing software, appropriate isolation, recoverable backups, and operational procedures that match the actual threat model.
We already have the hardware.
We already have Linux.
We already have Bitcoin Core.
And when necessary, we already have multisig.
The tools to build independent, understandable, long-term Bitcoin custody systems already exist.
We don't need an endless parade of specialized products to package those tools for us.
And we certainly don't need to make the entire hardware wallet industry an increasingly valuable honeypot for sophisticated attackers.
So the next time somebody tells you that the solution to another hardware wallet disaster is multi-vendor multisig, remember:
Three different logos don't eliminate the economics of targeted attacks.
And buying more security products isn't the same thing as improving your security.
Stop treating every new incident as an isolated failure of the wrong brand.
Start looking at the economic incentives created by the entire category.
Ditch the targeted black boxes.
Use generic hardware. Run minimal Linux. Trust Bitcoin Core.
Build your security around Bitcoin, not around the hardware wallet industrial complex.
Practical context

Core wallet encryption protects private key material; it does not hide every transaction record, public key or label. Keep the passphrase separately recoverable, make a fresh backup after encryption or relevant wallet changes, and test restoration. An outer encrypted archive adds privacy and another recovery step. Bitcoin Core wallet documentation.

title: Bitcoin Self-Custody Got Weird. It’s Time to Simplify It.
description: How hardware wallets, BIP39 ceremonies and fragmented security stacks became the default — and why Bitcoin Core on generic hardware deserves another look.

hero.alt: Bitcoin Self-Custody Got Weird. It’s Time to Simplify It. — Cover illustration

headings.text: Then Coldcard happened.
The attacker may be the most motivated reviewer in the room.
Security has economies of scale.
And then there is targetedness.
“But a generic laptop has Wi-Fi.”
“But USB is an attack surface.”
Then we arrived at dice.
BIP39 (kind of) solved a problem.
And no, this does not mean everyone should keep their life savings on their daily laptop.
Bitcoin Core doesn’t necessarily need to become everything.
AI changes this equation too.
I think Jack Mallers is noticing the same transition.
The future of Bitcoin self-custody may look strangely boring.
Maybe we optimized the wrong variable.

Practical context

blocks.html: How hardware wallets, BIP39 ceremonies and fragmented security stacks became the default — and why Bitcoin Core on generic hardware deserves another look.
For more than a decade, Bitcoin self-custody has been moving in one direction:
Buy a specialized device.
Generate 12 or 24 words.
Write them on paper or steel.
Learn derivation paths.
Learn fingerprints.
Learn coordinator exports.
Learn firmware updates.
Learn which wallet supports which hardware wallet.
Learn which version of which standard works with which other implementation.
Then, if something goes wrong, learn another ceremony for recovery.
Somewhere along the way we should probably ask a very simple question:
Did we actually make Bitcoin custody simpler and safer?
Or did we build an entire industry around compensating for complexity that we introduced ourselves?
I’ve spent the last few weeks arguing about this with hardware-wallet developers, wallet developers and Bitcoiners on X.
And the more I dig into it, the more convinced I become that we may have taken a very long detour.

blocks.alt: A cluttered collection of hardware wallets, seed plates, cables and manuals contrasts with a single ThinkPad running Bitcoin Core on a Mediterranean stone table.
blocks.caption: How much of the self-custody stack do we actually need?

blocks.html: Then Coldcard happened.
In July, a seed-generation flaw that had existed in affected Coldcard firmware since 2021 was exploited.
The problem wasn’t Bitcoin.
The attacker didn’t need to steal the devices.
The attacker didn’t need to compromise an air gap.
The problem was much simpler and much worse:
the wallets had generated weak secrets.

Coinkite itself now describes the incident as a firmware bug that weakened seed generation. Subsequent chain analysis reported roughly 1,816 BTC across more than 5,200 addresses swept during the attack waves. (COINKITE Blog)
The bug had survived for years in publicly inspectable firmware. (Source and licensing)
That sentence should permanently change the way Bitcoiners use the phrase:
“But it’s open source.”
Open source is enormously valuable.
But open source does not mean reviewed.
And reviewed does not mean reviewed by people with sufficient motivation, context and time to find the bug that matters.
That distinction is now impossible to ignore.
The attacker may be the most motivated reviewer in the room.
@jackmallers made essentially this point recently.
In his new @BTCsessions interview, the discussion around open-source security starts at about 57 minutes.
Then, around 1:02:04, he says something remarkably simple:
“Just use Bitcoin Core.”
His example is basically: go buy an ordinary laptop and use Bitcoin Core rather than assuming that a Bitcoin-specific device must inherently be safer.
His reasoning is more interesting than the recommendation itself.
Bitcoin Core has something a small security product cannot manufacture:
an enormous accumulated economic incentive to review it.
That deserves much more attention.

blocks.alt: Paths from diverse participants converge on a layered Bitcoin Core foundation, beside isolated towers representing separate wallet firmware stacks.
blocks.caption: Shared software lets security review compound. Every separate stack needs its own review.

blocks.html: Security has economies of scale.
Imagine Strike finds a bug in Bitcoin Core.
Coinbase benefits.
A miner benefits.
A custodian benefits.
I benefit.
You benefit.
Even Strike’s competitors benefit.
Nobody has to rebuild the security work from zero.
The next reviewer starts on top of everything reviewed before them.
This is a profoundly unusual incentive structure.
Bitcoin Core is depended upon by an enormous range of economically motivated actors. That gives those actors a shared interest in keeping the same underlying implementation correct.
The marginal review dollar compounds.
The marginal engineering hour compounds.
The marginal bug report compounds.
That does not make Bitcoin Core bug-free.
Nothing is.
But it creates a very different security economy.

Now compare that with an ecosystem containing dozens of hardware devices, firmware implementations, secure elements, companion apps, coordinators, update mechanisms, seed implementations and vendor-specific features.
Each additional stack needs its own review.
And every hardware manufacturer has a perfectly rational commercial incentive to differentiate its product from its competitors.
Security review fragments.
That is the opposite of compounding.
And then there is targetedness.
This is the part of the hardware-wallet threat model I think Bitcoiners systematically underestimate.
Suppose I order:
BITCOIN ULTRA SECURE SIGNING DEVICE™
The manufacturer knows what it is for.
The distributor knows what it is for.
Potentially the fulfillment company knows what it is for.
Anyone compromising that supply chain knows exactly what type of asset the device is likely to protect.
Now compare that with buying a random used ThinkPad.
There are millions upon millions of generic laptops in the world.
They belong to students, accountants, mechanics, schools, offices, grandmothers, programmers and dentists.
Nothing about the hardware tells anyone:
“This machine will protect Bitcoin.”
That enormous heterogeneous commodity market becomes a kind of hardware anonymity set.
Then I specialize the machine.
Not the manufacturer.
Not the distributor.
Me.

blocks.alt: A closely observed supply chain leads to a specialized signing device, while one ordinary laptop is selected from a vast, varied pool of generic computers.
blocks.caption: Buy an ordinary computer. Decide what it protects after it reaches your hands.

blocks.html: “But a generic laptop has Wi-Fi.”
So remove networking.
This is where I think people sometimes confuse generic hardware with generic configuration.
They are not the same thing.
I am currently building a stripped-down Debian image specifically for this purpose.
The offline version is essentially:
Debian + Bitcoin Core + the minimum required to operate the machine.
No browser.
No email client.
No LibreOffice.
No random desktop applications.
No networking in the signer configuration.
It can run stateless from a USB image in RAM.
Boot it.
Create or load a Core wallet.
Sign a PSBT.
Shut it down.

In a live session without configured persistence, the working wallet must be backed up to separate storage before shutdown. The release instructions will specify what persists in each boot and installation mode.
You can also install the same environment permanently onto an old laptop and effectively turn that commodity machine into a Bitcoin signing appliance.
If your threat model is sufficiently extreme, physically remove the Wi-Fi/Bluetooth hardware too.
But now notice what happened:
generic hardware became specialized hardware — after I bought it.
That distinction matters.
“But USB is an attack surface.”
Yes.
Everything is an attack surface.
QR parsers are attack surfaces.
Cameras are attack surfaces.
SD cards are attack surfaces.
USB stacks are attack surfaces.
Firmware update parsers are attack surfaces.
Your coordinator is an attack surface.
The question is never:
“Does this have an attack surface?”
The useful question is:
“What additional complexity am I introducing, and what threat am I buying that complexity to defend against?”
For most people I would rather start with the smallest understandable system and add complexity only when their actual threat model demands it.
If USB transport genuinely bothers you, harden the transport.
Use dedicated media.
Use hardware write protection.
For some extremely rare, extremely high-value movement, you could even use write-once optical media.
The point is not that one transport is magically perfect.
The point is that security architecture should be modular instead of ceremonial.
Then we arrived at dice.
This may be my favorite example of where Bitcoin custody culture has ended up.
After Coldcard, people understandably became nervous about entropy.
So now we have people sitting at tables rolling physical dice to generate Bitcoin secrets.
I understand the logic.
I just think we should zoom out for a second.

Bitcoin Core already has mature cryptographic randomness infrastructure. GetStrongRandBytes() incorporates operating-system entropy and is designed to fail if OS randomness cannot be obtained. Core key generation uses that strong RNG path. (GitHub)
Modern operating systems rely on CSPRNGs for security-critical randomness constantly.
Passwords.
Keys.
TLS.
Disk encryption.
Authentication.
Yet somehow, once Bitcoin enters the room, otherwise rational computer users become convinced that perhaps what the computer really needs is:
me, 256 coin flips and a worksheet.
You certainly can do it.
It is educational.
It might even be fun.
But I don’t think that should be the destination of mainstream self-custody.

blocks.alt: Dice, binary notes and seed-word worksheets contrast with a minimal Bitcoin Core laptop and a transparent flow from operating-system entropy to a wallet.
blocks.caption: More ceremony does not automatically mean better randomness.

blocks.html: BIP39 (kind of) solved a problem.
That doesn’t mean it should define Bitcoin custody forever.
Twelve or twenty-four words feel normal to Bitcoiners because we have spent years around them.
Step outside the bubble.
Imagine explaining self-custody to an otherwise competent 65-year-old business owner.
He knows how files work.
He knows what encryption means.
He understands making three backups.
He understands keeping copies in different locations.
He understands restoring a file.
Then tell him:
Here is an encrypted wallet.dat.
This file contains the wallet material you need.
We make redundant encrypted backups.
We separate the encryption secret.
Once a year we restore the wallet on a clean machine and prove the recovery procedure still works.
That mental model looks remarkably similar to normal computing.

Now explain seed words, BIP39 passphrases, derivation paths, account fingerprints, descriptor origins, compatibility between wallets, coordinator files and which parts of the wallet the seed does and does not reconstruct.
Which model is inherently more intuitive?
I think Bitcoiners have been inside the current paradigm so long that we no longer notice how strange it looks from outside.
And no, this does not mean everyone should keep their life savings on their daily laptop.
Quite the opposite.
Dedicated is the important word.
For a straightforward threat model:
generic dedicated computer
clean Linux
Bitcoin Core
For stronger isolation:
online Bitcoin Core node
offline Bitcoin Core signer
PSBT
The online machine has public wallet information and constructs transactions.
The offline machine owns the private keys and signs them.
Private keys never need to touch the online machine.
That is a remarkably simple security architecture.
And for single-sig, most of the ordinary wallet workflow is already available through Bitcoin Core’s GUI.
The CLI becomes necessary mainly when you want more advanced construction.
Multisig.
Descriptors.
Miniscript.
Timelocks.
Taproot policy trees.
Which brings us to the next part.
Bitcoin Core doesn’t necessarily need to become everything.
Its interfaces can become better.
For the last few months I’ve been building Core Explorer.
The idea is not to build another wallet.
It is to make the capabilities already available through Bitcoin Core understandable visually.
Imagine the good multisig workflow of Sparrow.
Recovery paths like Liana.
More advanced Miniscript and Taproot policies.
PSBT coordination.
But instead of introducing another key-management implementation underneath it, the GUI speaks to Bitcoin Core.
Core handles keys.
Core handles signing.
Core handles descriptors.
Core handles PSBTs.
The interface translates human intent into Core operations.
And yes — that interface itself becomes security-sensitive.
If a GUI incorrectly translates:
“Alice OR Bob after one year”
into the wrong policy, it does not matter that the cryptography underneath was perfect.
That translation layer needs tests and adversarial review too.
But this suggests a much healthier architecture:
put cryptography and key management in the most reviewed layer you have, and make everything above it as thin, inspectable and replaceable as possible.

blocks.alt: A thin graphical interface for spending policies sits above a substantial Bitcoin Core layer, supported by a generic laptop running minimal Linux.
blocks.caption: Core handles keys and signing. A thin, replaceable interface translates human intent into Core operations.

blocks.html: AI changes this equation too.
Ten years ago, telling a normal person to install Linux and learn a few commands was a real usability obstacle.
Today?
Paste the error into an AI.
Ask what the command does.
Ask it to explain every flag.
Ask it to inspect a configuration.
Ask it to teach you Linux interactively.
The cost of understanding computers has collapsed.
The cost of producing interfaces has collapsed too.
A small project can now prototype UX that previously required a funded software company.
That does introduce new risks — especially people shipping AI-generated code they do not understand.
But it also destroys one of the strongest historical arguments for vertically integrated hardware-wallet ecosystems:
“Normal people need us to package all of this for them.”
Maybe they did.
Maybe increasingly they won’t.
I think Jack Mallers is noticing the same transition.
What caught my attention in his latest interview was not merely that he recommended Bitcoin Core.
It was why.
His argument was essentially economic.
A tiny open-source repository can be public while still having relatively few economically motivated defenders.
Meanwhile an attacker may have an enormous financial incentive to find the one bug everyone else missed.
Bitcoin Core is different because so much of the Bitcoin economy already depends on it.
That creates scale.
That creates network effects around review.
And that creates something no “open source” badge alone can provide:
continuous economic demand for correctness.
This is the security property I think deserves far more attention after Coldcard.
The future of Bitcoin self-custody may look strangely boring.
No exotic device.
No Bitcoin-branded package arriving at your house.
No mandatory twelve-word initiation ceremony.
No proprietary ecosystem.
Maybe just:
An ordinary computer.
A minimal operating system.
Bitcoin Core.
A wallet file.
Good encryption.
Redundant backups.
A recovery drill.
And, when appropriate, another ordinary computer kept offline for signing.
That sounds less futuristic than a tiny signing gadget with secure elements, QR scanners and a dozen recovery standards.
Good.
Security should probably be boring.

blocks.alt: An older ThinkPad running Bitcoin Core rests beside two plain backup USB drives and a recovery-check date card on a sunlit stone desk overlooking the sea.
blocks.caption: An ordinary computer. Minimal Linux. Bitcoin Core. Encrypted backups. A recovery procedure you have actually tested.

blocks.html: Maybe we optimized the wrong variable.
For years the self-custody conversation has often been:
Which hardware wallet?
Which secure element?
Which seed storage plate?
Which multisig coordinator?
Which air gap?
Which entropy ceremony?
I increasingly think the better question is:
How much of this stack can I delete?
And underneath whatever remains:
Can Bitcoin Core do it instead?
Coldcard didn’t teach me that hardware wallets are evil.
It taught me something more interesting:
specialization is not automatically security.
Open source is not automatically review.
Air-gapped is not automatically safe.
DIY is not automatically untargeted.
More entropy ceremony is not automatically better randomness.
And more features are definitely not automatically more security.
Maybe the next era of Bitcoin self-custody is not about inventing another device.
Maybe it is about finally taking the software that already secures Bitcoin seriously as wallet infrastructure.
Generic hardware. Minimal Linux. Bitcoin Core. Everything else has to justify its existence.
