blocks.html: Multisig is an authorization policy, not a security level
Ask a Bitcoiner what multisig is for and the first answer will usually be some version of:
More security.

A small stack gets single-sig. A larger stack gets multisig. A very large stack gets multi-vendor multisig, with several hardware wallets, several seed phrases, several locations and enough recovery material to make the setup feel appropriately serious.
I understand how we got here. Some of these setups work. Some threat models genuinely benefit from multiple independent signers.
But I think the usual discussion starts one layer too late.

Much of modern Bitcoin custody is built around BIP39. Once the private key is represented primarily as 12 or 24 words, custody naturally becomes a problem of protecting those words. We stamp them into metal, hide them, distribute them, put them behind dedicated devices and eventually create several independent seeds so that losing or compromising one does not destroy the entire setup.
Multisig then gets pulled into that architecture as another form of redundancy.
I want to rewind the discussion to before all of that.
Start with Bitcoin Core.

A wallet contains private keys. The wallet can be encrypted. The encrypted wallet can be copied. Those copies can be stored in several places. Separately, Bitcoin has a spending condition that determines which signatures can move a coin.
That separation gives us a cleaner way to reason about custody.
Before asking whether we need single-sig or multisig, ask:
Who should have the authority to move the money?
Everything else follows from that.

blocks.alt: Single-Sig and Multisig from First Principles — Multisig is an authorization policy, not a security level illustration
blocks.caption: Multisig is not a higher security level. It changes the authorization structure.

blocks.html: Start by naming the problem
There is a simple engineering habit that is useful far beyond Bitcoin: do not add a mechanism until you know what problem it is solving.
Suppose you are worried that a storage device may die. You need another recoverable copy of the key material.

Suppose you are worried that somebody may steal one of those copies. Encryption can make possession of the file insufficient to recover the wallet, assuming the passphrase is strong and protected separately.

Suppose you are worried about malware on the machine that holds your keys. Then the environment that generates and uses those keys matters. A dedicated Linux machine used only for Bitcoin Core has a very different attack surface from the computer you use every day for email, browsing and downloaded software.
Now suppose your requirement is different: one independent signing authority must never be sufficient to spend the Bitcoin.
That is where multisig enters the picture.
These problems interact, but they are not interchangeable.
A backup answers a recovery problem.
Encryption addresses exposure of backup material.
A dedicated signer reduces the attack surface around key generation and signing.
Multisig changes the authorization condition.
If we collapse all of them into one vague category called security, it becomes very easy to use an expensive mechanism for a problem that had a simpler solution.

blocks.alt: Single-Sig and Multisig from First Principles — Start by naming the problem illustration
blocks.caption: Start with the failure mode, then choose the mechanism that addresses it.

blocks.html: What single-sig actually says
Take the simplest example.
Alice owns 1 BTC. One private key can produce the signature required to spend it, and Alice is the only person with access to that key.
That is single-sig.
Now Alice gives Bob access to the same wallet because she wants him to recover the Bitcoin if something happens to her.
The spending policy has not changed.
Alice can spend.
Bob can spend.
Either person can independently produce the one signature Bitcoin requires.
This is still single-sig.
That matters because people sometimes use single-sig as shorthand for “one person has access.”
That is not what the spending condition says.
It says that one valid signing authority is sufficient.
Alice and Bob might have an agreement that Bob will never touch the wallet while Alice is alive. That agreement can be perfectly sensible, especially inside a close family.
But the restriction exists between Alice and Bob. Bitcoin does not enforce it.
Bitcoin does not know that Bob is an heir. It does not know whether Alice is alive. It does not know whether Alice verbally approved the transaction.
It can only evaluate whether the spending condition has been satisfied.
That gives us our first useful separation: the social agreement and the cryptographic spending condition live at different layers.

blocks.alt: Single-Sig and Multisig from First Principles — What single-sig actually says illustration
blocks.caption: Human agreements determine what someone should do. Bitcoin only evaluates whether the spending condition was satisfied.

blocks.html: Backup is a different axis
Now put that single-sig wallet in Bitcoin Core.
Encrypt the wallet with a strong passphrase.
Make several copies of the encrypted wallet file.
Keep those copies on different media and in different locations. Protect the passphrase separately. Write recovery instructions. Test the recovery procedure.
You might end up with ten recoverable copies of the wallet.
You still have one signing authority.
Those ten files are not ten keys participating in a spending policy. They are ten ways of recovering the same key material.
A backup asks:
Can I recover this signer after a failure?
Multisig asks:
Which independent signers must approve this spend?
Once those questions are separated, both problems become easier to reason about.
Look at the marginal cost
There is another clue that backup and multisig belong to different layers.
Imagine that I already have three well-protected copies of an encrypted Bitcoin Core wallet and decide that I want a fourth.
Operationally, creating the fourth copy is trivial.
A fifth is also trivial.
So is a tenth.
The security cost is not literally zero. Every additional copy is another object that must remain encrypted, accounted for and included in the recovery plan.
But the marginal complexity is tiny.
I do not need another signing implementation.
I do not need another derivation path.
I do not need another independent wallet.
I do not need another person.
I do not need another device lifecycle that somebody will have to understand ten years from now.
Now compare that with adding an independent signer.
That signer needs a key.
The key needs backups.
Its recovery procedure must work.
The signer has to be included in the wallet policy.
The other participants need the information required to reconstruct that policy.
The signing workflow becomes more involved.
The additional work may be worth it because the extra signer changes the authorization policy in a way you genuinely need.
But if the only goal was:
I want another way to recover if something disappears.
then creating another independent signing authority is an extraordinarily expensive way to produce redundancy.
This is what I mean when I say:
Complexity is a security cost.
Simple systems are not automatically secure.
The point is that every moving part creates another assumption that has to remain true.

blocks.alt: Single-Sig and Multisig from First Principles — Look at the marginal cost illustration
blocks.caption: More backup copies add recovery paths. More independent signers add policy and operational complexity.

blocks.html: Build one good signer first
My preferred way to reason about custody starts with one complete signer.
For long-term cold storage, that could be a generic laptop with a clean Linux installation, dedicated to Bitcoin Core and kept offline.
The fact that the machine was manufactured as a general-purpose computer matters less to me than what it is allowed to do in this role.

If it never browses the web, never reads email, never installs random applications and never participates in everyday computing, its operational environment is much narrower than the phrase general-purpose computer suggests.
The Bitcoin Core wallet is encrypted.
There are redundant copies of the encrypted wallet.
The passphrase is protected separately.
Recovery instructions exist.
Most importantly, recovery is actually tested.
None of this makes the system invulnerable.
Commodity hardware can fail.
Linux can have bugs.
Bitcoin Core can have bugs.
Encryption depends on a strong secret.
Offline procedures can be executed badly.
What I like about this architecture is that each component has a legible job and the number of components remains small.
Generic hardware provides computation without adding a Bitcoin-specific device vendor and its own firmware, supply-chain and product lifecycle.
Linux provides the operating environment.
Bitcoin Core generates and uses the keys.
Encryption makes possession of the wallet file insufficient on its own.
Backups protect against loss of storage media.
A recovery drill checks whether the whole recovery path still works.
Once I understand that unit, I can reuse it.
That matters because multisig should be built from complete signers, not from half-understood key fragments whose only apparent purpose is to occupy another multisig slot.

blocks.alt: Single-Sig and Multisig from First Principles — Build one good signer first illustration
blocks.caption: Build one independently recoverable signer before combining several signers into a policy.

blocks.html: Now change the requirement
Suppose Alice and Bob jointly control 1 BTC.
They do not merely want both people to have access. They specifically want neither person to be able to spend alone.
Single-sig cannot enforce that rule.
A 2-of-2 multisig can.
Alice has one independent signer.
Bob has another.
The Bitcoin can move only when both signatures are present.
The multisig has not solved Alice's backups. Alice still needs to be able to recover her signer.
It has not solved Bob's backups either.
What changed is the relationship between their two authorities.
Bitcoin now enforces unanimous consent.
And unanimous consent has consequences.
If Alice wants to spend and Bob refuses, nothing moves.
It does not matter whether Bob is being reasonable. It does not matter whether they previously agreed that he should sign.
The policy says two signatures.
One signature is not enough.
That means a 2-of-2 gives both participants veto power.
Sometimes that is exactly what you want.

blocks.alt: Single-Sig and Multisig from First Principles — Now change the requirement illustration
blocks.caption: A 2-of-2 policy gives both signers veto power because every spend requires unanimous consent.

blocks.html: A third signer changes the decision rule
Now imagine Alice and Bob want shared control, but they do not want one disagreement or disappearance to freeze the treasury forever.
They add Carol.
Carol might be a mutually trusted friend, an attorney, another shareholder or a professional arbitrator. Her role is agreed before there is a dispute.
The policy becomes 2-of-3.
Alice and Bob can spend.
Alice and Carol can spend.
Bob and Carol can spend.
Nobody can spend alone.
And no single participant has unilateral veto power.
If Bob refuses a transaction that Alice believes falls within their prior agreement, Alice can take the issue to Carol.
Carol is not functioning as “backup number three.”
She is exercising an independent authorization role.
The third signer changes the decision rule.

blocks.alt: Single-Sig and Multisig from First Principles — A third signer changes the decision rule illustration
blocks.caption: The third signer changes who can form a valid quorum. That is a governance function.

blocks.html: What about losing one signer?
This is where the terminology gets slippery because multisig can absolutely create useful fault tolerance.
In a 2-of-3 wallet, losing one signer does not necessarily freeze the funds. The remaining two can still satisfy the policy.
Likewise, compromise of one signer alone does not give an attacker enough signatures to spend.
Those are real security properties.
But they do not make backup and multisig the same thing.
Each signer still needs a recovery plan.
Suppose Alice loses her signer. Bob and Carol can still move the money.
Now suppose Carol's wallet was never backed up correctly and her machine dies before they do so.
What looked like a comfortably redundant 2-of-3 has become an unspendable 1-of-3.
Threshold policies can tolerate failures between signers.
Backups make each signer recoverable within itself.
You have to reason about both layers.
Complexity has to earn its place
This is where I part ways with the current fashion for multi-vendor hardware-wallet multisig.
If multi-vendor means several Bitcoin-specific signing products from several Bitcoin hardware companies, I do not consider that an attractive architecture for my own long-term custody.
Yes, vendor diversity can reduce some common-mode risks.
But it also deliberately brings several Bitcoin-specific firmware stacks, device lifecycles, update mechanisms, supply chains and vendor assumptions into the same system.
I would rather avoid that entire category of dependency where I can.
If I ever wanted hardware diversity because of a specific threat model, I would much rather diversify across generic commodity computers used as dedicated signers.
Perhaps one signer runs on one class of ordinary laptop and another on different generic hardware, with both running a carefully controlled Linux and Bitcoin Core environment.
Even then, I would only take on that additional complexity for a narrow threat model that actually justified it.
I would not do it because “more vendors” has become synonymous with “more security.”
That distinction matters.
A complicated setup can feel safe precisely because it is complicated.
Five devices.
Five vendors.
Several seed plates.
Multiple locations.
Different firmware.
Different recovery procedures.
A coordinator tying them together.
There is a lot to look at, so the setup feels serious.
But a long-lived security system has to survive maintenance, not merely setup day.
What still works in ten years?
What information do you need to reconstruct the wallet?
What happens when one tool disappears?
Can another person recover the system after you are gone?
When did you last test the entire path?
Every extra dependency should have a specific job.
If you cannot say what failure it addresses, it may not belong in the design.
There is also an opportunity cost.
You have a finite amount of attention.

Every hour spent tracking another signer, another device family or another recovery path is an hour you did not spend restoring the wallet from backup and proving that your recovery procedure actually works.
I would rather own a simple system I regularly recover than a sophisticated system I am afraid to touch.

blocks.alt: Single-Sig and Multisig from First Principles — Complexity has to earn its place illustration
blocks.caption: Every moving part creates another assumption that must still hold when recovery day comes.

blocks.html: The psychological cost is real too
There is another reason complicated setups are difficult to revisit.
People become attached to things they build.

If you bought several devices, learned each workflow, stamped several seed plates, drove backups to different locations and spent weeks thinking through every combination, questioning the architecture later is uncomfortable.
You did a lot of work.
You may also have built part of your sense of safety around that work.
So when somebody questions one of those components, it can sound less like engineering criticism and more like an attack on the security you believe you created.
That reaction is understandable, especially when the asset at risk cannot be recovered through customer support.
But sunk effort is not a security property.
The useful question remains:
What job is this component doing?
If we can answer that for every part of a custody setup, the architecture becomes much easier to evaluate.
Multisig starts to look different when you call it governance
Consider the common policies again.
A 1-of-1 says one independent authority can spend.
A 2-of-2 requires unanimous approval between two authorities.
A 2-of-3 creates a quorum in which no individual can spend or veto alone.
A 3-of-5 creates another decision rule.
The interesting variable is how authority is distributed.
This becomes much more obvious when Bitcoin belongs to an organization rather than one individual.
I can use a real example from my own entrepreneurial life before Bitcoin became the center of my work.
I co-founded a startup with six individual co-founders.
Alongside us, one of the co-founders was a corporate investor.
Another was the nonprofit organization from which the startup had originally spun out.
So there were eight parties in the ownership structure:
six individuals,
one corporation,
and one nonprofit organization.
Imagine that company had been operating on a Bitcoin standard and that we had contributed Bitcoin capital to its treasury.
The useful question would not have been:
How many dollars are we storing? Is this enough for multisig?
The real questions would have been about authority.
How many of the six individual founders should approve a treasury transaction?
Should the investor have approval rights?
Should the nonprofit have a vote?
Could one group veto everyone else?
What happens if one founder disappears?
How should a dispute be resolved?
Then it becomes more interesting, because the corporate investor was not really one person.
It was a company with its own owners, management and internal rules.
The nonprofit also had its own governance structure.
So one “signer” at the company level could itself represent an entire authorization process underneath it.
A corporation could have its own internal multisig or spending policy.
The nonprofit could have another.
An individual founder could maintain one complete independent signer.
Those lower-level decisions could then feed into the higher-level treasury policy.
Now multisig is being used for the thing it is unusually good at:
turning a distribution of authority into a spending condition Bitcoin can enforce.

blocks.alt: Single-Sig and Multisig from First Principles — Multisig starts to look different when you call it governance illustration
blocks.caption: A real ownership structure from my pre-Bitcoin entrepreneurial life shows why multisig is fundamentally a governance tool.

blocks.html: This is where my criticism of BIP39 fits
BIP39 obviously works.
Millions of people have used mnemonic seeds successfully.
My criticism is architectural.
If the first lesson in custody is:
Your Bitcoin is these 12 or 24 words.
then custody becomes a problem of protecting those words.
Where do I store them?
What if the house burns down?
What if somebody finds the metal plate?
Should I split them?
Should I create another seed?
Should I use another device?
Should I put the seeds in different countries?
Should I put them into multisig?
The discussion starts at the recovery representation rather than at the spending policy.
I think that ordering has consequences.
It makes multisig easy to understand as “several seeds for more safety,” when a cleaner model treats the individual signer and the spending policy as separate layers.
Once those layers are clear, more advanced Bitcoin constructions become easier to reason about.
A timelocked recovery path is another condition describing when a different authorization becomes valid.
Miniscript becomes easier to understand because you are already thinking in spending conditions.
Taproot branches become easier to reason about because you already understand that different conditions can authorize the same coin.
Inheritance becomes a policy-design problem rather than merely a question of where to hide another copy of twelve words.
The same logic extends to companies, partnerships and federations.
This is what sound building blocks give you: the ability to add sophistication without losing track of what each component does.
Build complexity upward
There is a useful analogy with mathematics.
If somebody cannot understand an advanced result, staring at that result for another hour may not help.
The problem may sit several layers below it.
A definition was never clear.
An earlier operation became mechanical without being understood.
A concept was memorized rather than learned.
So you go backwards until you find the missing piece.
Fix it.
Then move forward again.
Custody works the same way.
If backup, encryption, signing and authorization are still tangled together in your head, adding a 3-of-5 multisig with recovery paths and timelocks will not untangle them.
It will bury the confusion under more machinery.
Get the primitive right first.
Build one signer that you understand.
Know exactly how its wallet is backed up.
Know how stolen backup media is protected.
Know how you restore it.
Actually restore it.
Then, if the spending policy requires two independent authorities, add another complete signer and require both.
If it requires arbitration, create a quorum.
If it requires delayed recovery, add that condition deliberately.
A system can become very sophisticated while the individual pieces remain understandable.
That is the kind of complexity I trust.

blocks.alt: Single-Sig and Multisig from First Principles — Build complexity upward illustration
blocks.caption: Advanced spending policies become easier to reason about once the underlying signer, backup and recovery model is clear.

blocks.html: Single-sig is not beginner mode
Once you see these layers separately, the usual maturity ladder stops making much sense.
A single owner may rationally choose single-sig even for a very large amount if the threat model, backup architecture and inheritance plan support that choice.
A small business may rationally need multisig for a much smaller amount because no one employee or partner should have unilateral authority over company funds.
The difference is not sophistication.
The difference is the spending requirement.
A well-designed single-sig setup can include an offline signer, strong wallet encryption, redundant backups, a separately protected passphrase, tested recovery and clear inheritance instructions.
A badly designed multisig can still be fragile.
Counting keys tells you very little without understanding the systems behind them and the policy connecting them.
Start with authority
If I were designing a Bitcoin custody setup from scratch, I would not begin by choosing a hardware wallet.
I would not begin by deciding whether I want 12 words or 24.
And I would not begin by deciding whether the amount of Bitcoin is “big enough for multisig.”
I would write down who should be capable of authorizing a transaction.
If one person should have that authority, I would design one signer and make its recovery exceptionally good.
If two people must approve every transaction, I would use a policy that enforces that.
If two partners need an independent arbitrator, I would design a quorum around those three authorities.
If a board controls the funds, I would translate the board's actual decision rules into the spending policy as closely as Bitcoin allows.
Then I would solve backup, encryption, signer security and recovery for every key participating in that policy.
The order matters because it keeps different problems at the layer where they belong.
Recovery stays a recovery problem.
Signer security stays a signer problem.
Authorization stays a spending-policy problem.
And every new component has to explain why it exists.
When you can do that, multisig stops looking like an upgrade from single-sig.
It becomes a tool for expressing something much more precise:
who must agree before the money moves.

blocks.alt: Single-Sig and Multisig from First Principles — Start with authority illustration
blocks.caption: Start with the people who should control the money. Choose the implementation after the spending rule is clear.

blocks.html: How Bitcoiners Turned a Simple Security Problem Into a Security Ritual
Bitcoiners made self-custody much more complicated than it needed to be.
The original problem was real, but extremely simple:
People were using Bitcoin wallets on computers that could be compromised.
Your daily laptop might contain hundreds of applications, browser extensions, email attachments, proprietary software, old packages, random downloads, and possibly malware.
Of course that is not the ideal environment in which to generate and protect Bitcoin private keys.
But notice what the actual problem was.
The problem was not:
General-purpose computers cannot securely hold Bitcoin keys.
The problem was:
You are using Bitcoin on an unsafe computer.
The obvious first-principles solution should therefore have been equally simple.
Take another computer.
Wipe it.
Install a clean operating system.
Install Bitcoin Core.
Dedicate that machine to Bitcoin.
If your threat model requires stronger isolation, keep the signing machine offline and move PSBTs between the online coordinator and offline signer.
Problem solved.
Instead, many Bitcoiners took a very different path.

blocks.alt: The Hardware Wallet Detour — How Bitcoiners Turned a Simple Security Problem Into a Security Ritual illustration
blocks.caption: The problem was never generic hardware. It was using Bitcoin on a dirty, potentially compromised daily computer.

blocks.html: The detour begins

In 2014, Trezor launched what it describes as the world's first hardware wallet. Two of Trezor's founders, Marek Palatinus and Pavol Rusnak, were also among the authors of BIP39, proposed in 2013 as a standardized human-readable mnemonic representation for deterministic-wallet entropy. (Trezor)
The hardware-wallet model made intuitive sense at first.
If the host computer might be compromised, put the keys into a little dedicated computer and sign somewhere else.
But that architectural choice also created another problem.
You no longer had a normal Bitcoin Core wallet environment where the complete wallet could simply be treated as a wallet artifact.
So the industry increasingly normalized another mental model:
Export the root secret and make the human responsible for preserving it.
And that was the beginning of a very long detour.

blocks.alt: The Hardware Wallet Detour — The detour begins illustration
blocks.caption: Instead of isolating Bitcoin on clean generic hardware, we created an entire specialized hardware-wallet industry — and years of new complexity.

blocks.html: Imagine if Excel worked like BIP39
The absurdity becomes much easier to see if you apply the same philosophy to normal computing.
Imagine you're working on an important encrypted Excel spreadsheet.
Today the mental model is completely obvious.
You finish your work.
You click:
File → Save
If the file is sensitive, you encrypt it.
If you want another copy, you back it up.
Years later, you open Excel and click:
File → Open
Nobody thinks this is remarkable.
Now imagine Microsoft introduced the Bitcoin Hardware Wallet School of File Management™.
You finish your spreadsheet and click Save.
Excel responds:
Great. Instead of actually preserving your workbook, here are 24 words representing the master entropy from which part of the workbook can theoretically be reconstructed.
Please engrave them into steel.
But wait.
Those words are not actually the spreadsheet.
So please also record:
which workbook schema you were using,
which spreadsheet format was active,
which version of Excel created it,
how worksheets and relationships were structured,
whether macros existed,
which formula-engine behavior was expected,
which metadata another application would require,
and perhaps export a chunk of XML describing enough of the workbook structure that another implementation might reconstruct it later.
Maybe also open Excel's source code, locate whichever serialization rules your particular workbook depended upon, print the relevant section and store it next to your steel plate.
For additional security, you can add another secret to your 24 words.
Except it doesn't encrypt the 24 words.
Instead it deterministically produces an entirely different workbook.
Every possible passphrase produces a valid workbook.
Please make sure you remember which one was yours.
Twenty years later, your children can enjoy reconstructing the spreadsheet.
And computer-security people would proudly tell you:
“See how simple this is? You only need 24 words.”
Nobody would accept this for Excel.
They would ask:
Why can't I just save the damn file?
Exactly.

blocks.alt: The Hardware Wallet Detour — Imagine if Excel worked like BIP39 illustration
blocks.caption: If normal software handled backups the way Bitcoiners handle seed phrases, nobody would tolerate it.

blocks.html: Bitcoin Core already has the sane mental model
Bitcoin Core's model is conceptually boring.
That is a feature.
You have a wallet.
You encrypt the wallet.
You back up the wallet.
You restore the wallet.
The backup can preserve the wallet data as a coherent artifact rather than forcing the user to reduce the entire object to one naked human-readable root secret.
And critically, the user-facing backup primitive does not need to become more complicated as the wallet becomes more sophisticated.
A simple wallet?
Backup Wallet.
A wallet containing imported descriptors or more sophisticated policy information?
The desired abstraction remains:
Backup Wallet.
Later:
Restore Wallet.
The complexity belongs inside the software.
Not inside the user's head.
A better wallet becoming more sophisticated should not mean that inheritance and recovery become more sophisticated too.
That is backwards.
BIP39 made the user responsible for wallet archaeology
The moment the industry taught users that “the seed phrase is the wallet,” we introduced a conceptual error.
A root secret is not necessarily the entire wallet.
The BIP39 specification itself demonstrates the issue.

A 12-word BIP39 mnemonic represents 128 bits of entropy plus a 4-bit checksum. A 24-word mnemonic represents 256 bits plus an 8-bit checksum. But those words do not inherently tell future software everything about how the wallet was used. The current BIP39 document itself lists the lack of a versioning scheme as a shortcoming and notes that the mnemonic originally provided no way to determine which address format should be used; descriptors mitigate that problem precisely by preserving more wallet information outside the seed. (GitHub)
That proves the point.
The seed is not the wallet.
Now add multisig.
Add different script types.
Add account structures.
Add timelocks.
Add more sophisticated spending conditions.
Suddenly recovery can become an archaeology exercise:
What wallet software generated this?
Which path?
Which account?
Which descriptor?
Which cosigners?
Which policy?
Which assumptions?
The supposedly universal backup gets less complete precisely as the wallet gets more interesting.
That is an awful abstraction.

blocks.alt: The Hardware Wallet Detour — BIP39 made the user responsible for wallet archaeology illustration
blocks.caption: A root secret is only one component. The wallet also has descriptors, policy, script assumptions, metadata and recovery context.

blocks.html: Then we patched the patch with a passphrase
There was another obvious problem.
If your 12 or 24 words are the naked master secret, redundancy becomes dangerous.
Put the words in one place and you have a single backup.
Put identical copies in ten places and now you have ten locations containing the complete root secret.
So another ritual became popular:
Add a BIP39 passphrase.
But here again the user's intuitive mental model can be wrong.
The passphrase does not simply encrypt the mnemonic like encrypting a file.
BIP39 uses the mnemonic and "mnemonic" + passphrase through PBKDF2 to derive a seed, and every possible passphrase produces a valid seed. (GitHub)
So now the supposedly elegant “12 words on paper” recovery model may actually mean:
12 or 24 words.
Plus another sufficiently strong passphrase.
Stored separately.
Plus whatever wallet metadata is needed for recovery.
Plus recovery instructions for your heirs.
We solved a backup problem by turning users into part-time cryptographic archivists.
Then came entropy theater
The rituals did not stop there.

After weaknesses in hardware-wallet entropy generation received renewed attention, Bitcoin discussion increasingly shifted toward users manually generating randomness with dice, cards, and elaborate entropy ceremonies.
There is nothing inherently wrong with independently generated randomness.
But the discussion often loses perspective.

Modern operating systems already provide cryptographically secure randomness. Bitcoin Core's strong RNG explicitly incorporates OS entropy such as getrandom() or /dev/urandom, mixes additional sources, and is designed to fail if the OS RNG fails. (GitHub)
We trust operating systems and reviewed cryptographic software to generate high-strength passwords, encryption keys, SSH keys and countless other secrets every day.

Password managers routinely generate cryptographically strong secrets. KeePassXC, for example, provides both random-password and passphrase generation and even supports external EFF-style wordlists. (KeePassXC)
Yet somehow Bitcoin convinced itself that a person rolling physical dice is intrinsically more serious than mature cryptographic software running on a freshly installed dedicated Linux system.
Rolling dice does not eliminate trust.
Eventually those dice results still have to enter hardware, firmware and software and be transformed into Bitcoin private keys.
Bitcoin is software.
Not physical gold.

blocks.alt: The Hardware Wallet Detour — Then came entropy theater illustration
blocks.caption: Manual ritual is not automatically stronger security. Mature operating systems and reviewed cryptographic software already solve secure randomness extremely well.

blocks.html: We also chose a surprisingly inefficient human encoding
BIP39 uses a 2,048-word list.
That gives exactly 11 bits per word.
A 12-word mnemonic therefore contains 128 bits of entropy plus its checksum. (GitHub)
Compare that with an EFF-style Diceware list containing 7,776 words.
Each independently selected word carries about 12.9 bits of entropy.
So roughly ten truly random words from a 7,776-word list already reach approximately 129 bits.

In other words, if humans really need to remember or separately store a strong passphrase, there are already mature password-management conventions that can encode comparable strength with fewer words.
The Bitcoin industry did not discover some uniquely optimal human-secret format.
It standardized one format around wallet recovery and then built an enormous ritual culture around it.
Then there is the checksum illusion
People also frequently talk about BIP39's checksum as if it somehow validates the security of the generated secret.
It does not.
The checksum only validates consistency with the mnemonic encoding.
BIP39 takes the generated entropy, appends a short SHA256-derived checksum, and maps the result into words. For 12 words the checksum is only four bits; for 24 words it is eight. (GitHub)
If the underlying entropy generation procedure was weak, the checksum does not magically make it strong.
A perfectly checksummed mnemonic can still originate from catastrophically weak randomness.
Which brings us to Coldcard.
“But the firmware is public”
One of the standard answers to specialized-device risk is:
“But the firmware is open source.”
Fine.
Publicly inspectable source is clearly preferable to opaque firmware.

Coldcard publishes its firmware source, documents reproducible builds and makes hardware information available for inspection. Its current licensing is better described precisely as source-available/publicly inspectable because it adds the Commons Clause to MIT terms. (Coldcard)
But here is the uncomfortable lesson:
Public code does not review itself.

A Coldcard firmware flaw dating to March 2021 weakened randomness for affected wallets. According to TRM Labs' August 2026 analysis, a build/configuration problem caused affected devices to fall back to weak software randomness rather than the intended hardware entropy source, reducing effective strength on some devices from 128 bits to as little as roughly 40 bits. (TRM Labs)
The flaw survived for about five years.
Then attackers exploited the weak seeds.
By August 5, TRM reported roughly 1,816 BTC, worth around $116 million at the time, drained from more than 5,200 addresses. (TRM Labs)
Stop for a moment and think about what that means.
The firmware was available to inspect.
The product was explicitly marketed as a specialized Bitcoin security device.
Its users performed all the rituals.
Air gaps.
Seed backups.
Dedicated hardware.
Specialized signing.
Yet the catastrophic entropy problem remained in the specialized security stack for years.
Why?
Not because source visibility is useless.
Because source visibility and actual security review are completely different things.

blocks.alt: The Hardware Wallet Detour — “But the firmware is public” illustration
blocks.caption: Source visibility matters, but it is not the same as deep review. Security depends on how many capable people are economically incentivized to actually look.

blocks.html: Security is economic
This is the part I think the hardware-wallet conversation misunderstands most deeply.
Software is not secure because someone put the source on GitHub.
Software becomes safer because sufficiently capable people have sufficiently strong incentives to scrutinize it.
Imagine you personally had to secure $1 billion of Bitcoin.
Would spending $100,000 on an independent security review sound expensive?
Of course not.
You might happily spend several hundred thousand dollars.
You would review the signing environment.
You would examine builds.
You would test recovery.
You might audit firmware.
You might audit hardware.
You would model supply chains.
Because the marginal cost of review is tiny relative to the economic value being protected.
But then another economic insight becomes obvious.
You would not want your expensive security review to begin from zero.
You would want to start with software that already had:
years of public scrutiny,
many expert contributors,
many independent reviewers,
large amounts of economic value depending on it,
a mature release process,
and a long adversarial history.
Then your next security dollar compounds all the review that happened before you.
That is the enormous advantage of Bitcoin Core.

blocks.alt: The Hardware Wallet Detour — Security is economic illustration
blocks.caption: The more value a system protects, the stronger the incentive to review it. Build on software that already has years of scrutiny behind it.

blocks.html: The economics of Bitcoin Core are different
Bitcoin Core is not merely another wallet application.

It is the reference implementation used across the Bitcoin ecosystem and has accumulated years of scrutiny from contributors, infrastructure operators, businesses, miners, exchanges and technically sophisticated users.
Its release process goes unusually far into the software-supply-chain problem.

Bitcoin Core's Guix build infrastructure is designed to make releases reproducible and bootstrappable rather than requiring users to blindly trust one person's precompiled binaries. Independent builders can reproduce release binaries and publish signed attestations of the hashes they obtained. (GitHub)

The official Bitcoin Core download documentation describes this explicitly: multiple contributors can independently reproduce identical binaries and cryptographically attest to their checksums. (Bitcoin Core)
That changes the economic structure of trust.
You are not beginning your security analysis with a $200 consumer gadget produced by one company.
You are adding your own verification on top of an enormous pre-existing body of review.
That matters.
Hardware-wallet economics are different
Now compare that with a retail hardware wallet.
A normal customer buys a device for perhaps a few hundred dollars.
They are not going to spend $100,000 independently auditing its firmware.
They are certainly not going to decap chips, inspect silicon, trace the supply chain and independently validate every hardware claim.
They assume someone else did the difficult work.
Maybe someone did.
Maybe several researchers did.
Maybe nobody looked closely enough at precisely the failure that matters to them.
And this creates a strange economic mismatch.
The vendor has a commercial incentive to explain the threats its product solves.
Compromised desktop?
Dangerous.
USB?
Dangerous.
Browser malware?
Dangerous.
Air-gap attack?
Dangerous.
Supply-chain seal?
Use our special packaging.
Entropy?
Perform our special ritual.
And suddenly generic hardware begins to sound impossibly dangerous.
But what receives much less attention are all the attack surfaces that exist because the specialized Bitcoin product now exists.
The targetedness problem
A hardware wallet is not only a security device.
It is information.
Buying one tells someone something economically valuable:
This person probably owns Bitcoin.
The hardware-wallet manufacturer may know.
The payment processor may know.
The fulfillment provider may know.
The shipping company may know.
The email marketing system may know.
Support infrastructure may know.
And when those databases are breached, leaked or abused, the attack does not have to involve cracking a secure element or discovering a zero-day.
In many cases that would be economically stupid.
Why spend millions developing an exploit if you can simply impersonate customer support?
Send a convincing security alert.
Send a fake firmware update.
Tell the target their wallet is compromised.
Ask them to “verify” their backup.
Build trust over weeks.
Run a recovery scam.
Run a SIM attack.
Attempt extortion.
Or, in the worst case, use the shipping address to turn a digital security problem into a physical one.
The hardware wallet can remain cryptographically flawless while its owner becomes dramatically easier to attack.
That is targetedness.

blocks.alt: The Hardware Wallet Detour — The targetedness problem illustration
blocks.caption: A hardware wallet is not only a security device. It is also a signal that tells vendors, databases and potentially attackers that you likely own Bitcoin.

blocks.html: Commodity hardware changes the economics
Now compare that with a used ThinkPad.
There are enormous numbers of generic laptops circulating through a gigantic commodity market.
Nobody looking at Lenovo's customer database knows:
This person bought this laptop specifically to secure Bitcoin.
It might belong to an accountant.
A student.
A developer.
A grandmother.
A warehouse worker.
A dentist.
A Bitcoin holder.
Nobody knows.
Could generic hardware theoretically contain malicious hardware?
Of course.
But security is not about listing theoretically possible attacks.
It is about threat models and economics.

Seeding random commodity laptops at the hardware level in the hope that one of them eventually becomes an offline Bitcoin signer has radically different economics from targeting a known population of specialized devices whose entire purpose is storing valuable cryptographic keys.
And the obvious second-hand software risk is trivial to address.
Wipe the machine.
Install Linux from verified installation media.
Install Bitcoin Core.
Done.
The black-box irony
Hardware wallets were supposed to eliminate trust in general-purpose computers.
Instead, they frequently move trust into a much smaller specialized stack.
Custom hardware.
Custom firmware.
Custom bootloaders.
Secure elements.
Specialized displays.
Firmware-update procedures.
Companion applications.
Manufacturing.
Shipping.
Vendor infrastructure.
Even when schematics are available, independently validating the actual physical device in your hand at chip and supply-chain level is far more expensive than reading source code.
And this brings us straight back to economics.
For a billion-dollar custody operation, perhaps that expense makes sense.
For a retail buyer with $20,000 of Bitcoin?
It obviously does not.
The retail buyer is therefore still trusting.
They have simply been taught to call the trust ceremony “verification.”
Multi-vendor multisig does not magically remove this
The latest version of the ritual often says:
Use multisig with hardware wallets from multiple vendors.
To be clear, multisig can absolutely reduce important classes of risk.
A compromised key does not necessarily compromise the wallet.
One defective device need not destroy security.
Different implementations can reduce correlated failure.
Those are real advantages.
But security has multiple dimensions.
On the targetedness and operational-complexity axis, buying devices from three specialized Bitcoin companies can mean:
three manufacturers,
three customer databases,
three shipping relationships,
three firmware ecosystems,
three update procedures,
three vendor lifetimes,
three sets of recovery assumptions,
and more complexity for whoever inherits the setup.
So you can reduce one risk while increasing another.
The tradeoff needs to be modeled honestly.
If you wanted to manufacture a truly gigantic operational headache for yourself, you could simply buy one device from every hardware-wallet manufacturer in existence.
There is certainly no shortage of them.
You would create a beautiful collection of specialized dependencies while repeatedly telling companies and third parties:
Hello. I own Bitcoin. And apparently enough Bitcoin that I take custody very seriously.
Once you see the targetedness problem, you cannot unsee it.
Complexity is itself a security cost
This is the principle underlying almost everything above.
Every additional component introduces:
another assumption,
another failure mode,
another thing to document,
another thing an heir must understand,
another dependency that must still exist ten years from now,
another opportunity to make a mistake.
Bitcoiners frequently treat complexity as evidence of sophistication.
It is often the opposite.
Real security engineering tries very hard to remove things.
A security system with five moving parts is not automatically better than one with two.

A ritual involving steel plates, dice, multiple vendors, firmware verification, derivation-path documentation, passphrase separation, descriptor backup and inheritance instructions is not automatically safer because it feels serious.
Sometimes you have simply created more ways to fail.
Go back to the original problem
Strip away more than a decade of accumulated hardware-wallet culture and ask the original question again.
I do not want my Bitcoin private keys on my potentially compromised daily computer. What should I do?
My answer is almost embarrassingly simple.
Get another computer.
It does not need to be fancy.
Generic commodity hardware is fine.
A used ThinkPad is fine.
Install a clean, boring Linux distribution such as Debian Stable.
Verify Bitcoin Core.
Generate the wallet there.
Encrypt it.
Back it up.
Test the restore.
Do not use that machine for random daily computing.
If the value and threat model justify stronger isolation, make it an offline signer and move PSBTs between systems.
That solves the actual problem.
And the backup should remain boring
The final irony is that we spent years teaching Bitcoiners elaborate recovery rituals around something computer users already understand perfectly.
Files.
Your wallet should be treated as a coherent artifact.
Encrypt it.
Back it up redundantly.
Keep the encryption secret separate where appropriate.
Periodically test that your backups restore correctly.
The computer industry has spent decades figuring out how to preserve files.
You can copy an encrypted artifact to multiple USB drives.
Optical media.
SSDs.
Remote storage.
Different buildings.
Different jurisdictions.
Whatever redundancy matches your threat model.
Because the file is encrypted, redundancy does not have the same security property as making ten naked copies of the root secret.
And when somebody needs to recover it, the desired user experience should remain:
Restore Wallet.
Not:
“Here are twelve words. Good luck reconstructing what Grandpa was doing in 2034.”
Security should compound, not restart from zero
This is ultimately why I keep coming back to Bitcoin Core.
I want my own security efforts to build on top of the largest possible accumulation of previous security work.
I want boring commodity hardware.
A mature operating system.
A clean dedicated environment.
The most reviewed Bitcoin implementation available to me.
Reproducible builds.
Independent attestations.
A normal encrypted-file backup model.
And as few Bitcoin-specific dependencies as possible.
Then, if the amount of Bitcoin being protected becomes large enough to justify additional independent audits, those marginal security dollars compound an already enormous existing body of work.
That is how security should scale.
Not by inventing another gadget.
Not by adding another ritual.
Not by creating another human-readable master secret.
Not by adding another vendor.
Keep it simple
Hardware wallets began by trying to solve a legitimate problem.
But I think Bitcoin took the wrong architectural lesson from that problem.
The answer to:
“My computer might be compromised.”
did not need to become:
“Let's create an entire specialized hardware industry, export wallet root secrets into human-readable words, and teach users an increasingly elaborate set of security ceremonies.”
It could simply have been:
Don't use the compromised computer.
Use clean dedicated hardware.
Use a mature operating system.
Use Bitcoin Core.
Keep your backups boring.
Test recovery.
And remove everything you do not need.
Generic hardware. Linux. Bitcoin Core.
Everything else should have to justify the additional trust, complexity, targetedness and attack surface it introduces.

blocks.alt: The Hardware Wallet Detour — Keep it simple illustration
blocks.caption: Generic hardware. Linux. Bitcoin Core. Fewer specialized dependencies, less targetedness, less complexity.

blocks.html: Practical context

Core wallet encryption protects private key material; it does not hide every transaction record, public key or label. Keep the passphrase separately recoverable, make a fresh backup after encryption or relevant wallet changes, and test restoration. An outer encrypted archive adds privacy and another recovery step. Bitcoin Core wallet documentation.

blocks.alt: We Made Bitcoin Self-Custody Harder Than It Had to Be — The seed phrase was supposed to simplify recovery. Instead, it taught people to treat one plaintext object as the wallet, the backup and the single point of failure. illustration
blocks.caption: We spent a decade improving the durability of the backup without asking whether we had chosen the right object to back up.

blocks.html: This article began as a voice-dictated reply to someone who made what sounds like a completely reasonable argument:

If an attacker gets my encrypted Bitcoin Core wallet file and the passphrase that unlocks it, I lose my bitcoin. If an attacker gets his BIP39 mnemonic and the passphrase attached to it, he loses his bitcoin. Therefore, the threat model is identical, and the rest is simply personal preference.
At the very end of the failure chain, that is true.
If the attacker obtains everything required to spend, the attacker wins.

But the fact that two systems can reach the same final failure does not make their threat models identical. It tells us nothing about how many ways each system can reach that failure, what each individual backup object gives an attacker, how safely the components can be copied, how easily ordinary people can understand the model, or how the system behaves when someone makes a perfectly normal human mistake.
Those are not secondary details.
They are the security architecture.
And the more I think about this, the more convinced I become that we spent the last decade teaching people a mental model that made Bitcoin self-custody far harder than it needed to be.
Remember the first time you explained a seed phrase
If you have ever orange-pilled a friend, helped a family member buy bitcoin, or walked a complete beginner through self-custody, you probably know this conversation.
First, you show them the wallet.
Then the wallet shows them twelve or twenty-four words.

You explain that those words are extremely important. They must never lose them, because losing them could mean losing the bitcoin. They must never show them to anyone, because anyone who sees them may be able to take the bitcoin. They should not photograph them, type them into a phone, email them to themselves, save them in cloud storage or place them inside an ordinary digital document.
Paper can burn or decay, so perhaps they should engrave the words into steel.
They should probably have more than one backup, because one location can flood, burn or become inaccessible.
But they should not make too many copies, because each additional copy is another place from which the entire wallet can potentially be stolen.
If they want stronger protection, they can add a BIP39 passphrase.
But now they must preserve that too.

They must not store it with the mnemonic. They must not forget it. Their heirs must understand that the mnemonic without the passphrase may lead to a different wallet. A typo in the passphrase does not produce a clear “wrong password” error; it produces another perfectly valid wallet that happens to be empty.
By the end of the explanation, the beginner is no longer looking at a simple way to hold bitcoin.

He is looking at a small object that must survive fire, water, theft, accidental destruction, memory loss, family confusion and his own death, while remaining invisible to every other human being for the rest of his life.
Then we smile and tell him:
Welcome to sovereignty.

I have had some version of this conversation repeatedly, and I suspect many Bitcoiners have too. I have seen the moment when a person understands that one piece of paper may effectively control the savings, and the immediate conclusion is almost always the same:
Bitcoin self-custody must be incredibly difficult.
You must be technically sophisticated.
You must be unusually paranoid.
You must become a security expert before you can safely hold your own money.
For years, I accepted that conclusion too.
Now I think we blamed Bitcoin for complexity that came from the backup architecture we chose.

blocks.alt: We Made Bitcoin Self-Custody Harder Than It Had to Be — Remember the first time you explained a seed phrase illustration
blocks.caption: We came to treat the anxiety produced by the seed model as an unavoidable property of Bitcoin itself.

blocks.html: The key became the vault
BIP39 is not nonsense, and it was not created without a real purpose.

It takes computer-generated entropy, adds a checksum and represents the result as a sequence of words that a human can transcribe. Its own specification presents the mnemonic as a human-readable way to transport computer-generated randomness, and explicitly says that it is not intended as a way to turn a sentence invented by the user into a wallet. That was genuinely useful. It made recovery portable, inspectable and interoperable across implementations.
The problem is what happened to that useful mechanism once it became the dominant mental model for self-custody.
The careful technical description became:
These words are your wallet.
That sentence is easy to remember, but it also concentrates an extraordinary amount of authority in one highly portable, recognizable, human-readable object.

Without an effective independent passphrase, a BIP39 mnemonic is a bearer secret. Someone who copies it does not need to steal the original. The owner receives no notification. There is no rate limit, no tamper alarm and no failed-login counter. The attacker can restore it somewhere else, at another time, using another wallet.
Steel improves durability.
It does not change that authority.

A steel plate may survive a house fire, but it can also be photographed in seconds. It may remain readable for generations, but so will the secret for anyone who finds it. It protects the user from losing the backup by making the backup harder to destroy, while doing nothing to reduce the consequences of somebody else discovering it.
This produces a basic contradiction.
For availability, we want more copies.
For secrecy, we want fewer copies.

Suppose I engrave the same unprotected mnemonic onto three steel plates and place them in three locations. I have improved my protection against fire, flooding and accidental loss. At the same time, I have created three locations from which the complete root secret can be copied.
One side of the system becomes safer as the other side becomes more exposed.
The usual answer is to add a strong BIP39 passphrase.
That can materially improve the setup. I do not deny it. A well-generated passphrase, preserved separately from the mnemonic, can prevent disclosure of the words alone from being sufficient to spend.
But notice what we have done.
We repaired the single-bearer-secret problem by creating a two-component system and telling the user to keep the components separate.
The simple promise of “just preserve these words” has now become:

Preserve the mnemonic, preserve a strong independent passphrase, never colocate them, make both available to your heirs, remember that every passphrase generates a valid wallet, preserve any additional wallet-policy information, and test the complete recovery.
That can be a strong architecture in expert hands.
It is not the simple twelve-word story we use to onboard beginners.

BIP39 also preserves root-secret material, not necessarily the complete wallet context. The mnemonic alone does not describe every script type, derivation structure, account, multisig policy, descriptor or recovery branch that future software may need. For a simple and conventional single-signature wallet, software can often search common paths. As the wallet becomes more complex, “I still have the words” becomes less equivalent to “I have preserved the wallet.”
The Core model finally gave me a simpler explanation
When I recently went back and tested Bitcoin Core as a wallet from beginning to end, something clicked.
Create the wallet.
Encrypt it.
Make a backup.
Restore it.
Construct a PSBT on another machine.
Sign it offline.
The workflow was not perfect, and Core’s interface still needs serious work, but the security model itself was much easier to reason about than I had expected.
The simplest explanation is this:
The encrypted wallet file is the vault.
The passphrase is the key to the vault.
The vault can be copied.

I can keep redundant copies of the encrypted wallet file on different media and in different locations: USB storage, optical media, another drive, another computer or encrypted remote storage, depending on my threat model.
If one copy becomes unreadable, I have others.

If somebody obtains one encrypted wallet backup, he has not automatically obtained spending authority, provided the private keys are protected by strong wallet encryption and the passphrase has enough entropy.

The passphrase is backed up separately. Use KeePassXC on the prepared, trusted computer: six independently generated random words by default, or eight if memorizing two extra words is comfortable for you. It can also have redundant copies, provided they are never stored together with the corresponding wallet backup.
Someone finding only the passphrase cannot reconstruct the wallet.
Someone finding only the encrypted wallet backup cannot unlock the private keys without the passphrase.
The rule becomes:
Keep the vault and the key apart.
That is a security heuristic ordinary people already understand.

Bitcoin Core’s wallet encryption does not make the entire wallet database an opaque blob. Public keys, transactions and some wallet metadata may remain visible, so the backup should still be treated as sensitive. But encrypted private-key material is not equivalent to a plaintext root bearer secret, and the wallet file can preserve substantially more of the actual wallet state than a bare mnemonic does. Bitcoin Core also supports constructing and signing PSBTs, allowing the private-key wallet to remain on a separate offline machine.
The final part is not optional:
Restore it.
A backup that has never been restored is a theory.

I want to periodically load a copy, verify the expected wallet, construct a transaction, inspect it, sign it in the intended environment and make sure the full procedure still works. The goal is not to feel reassured because I own an indestructible object. The goal is to know that I can recover and spend.

blocks.alt: We Made Bitcoin Self-Custody Harder Than It Had to Be — The Core model finally gave me a simpler explanation illustration
blocks.caption: Redundancy no longer requires making several immediately spendable copies of the same plaintext secret.

blocks.html: “You were not supposed to do that” is not a security model
Operational security is not separate from wallet design.
The onboarding flow is part of the security architecture because it determines which mistakes normal people are likely to make.

I recently performed a small experiment in a popular desktop wallet. I selected the BIP39 software-wallet path and began entering words manually. I was able to supply a user-chosen mnemonic that the wallet accepted once the checksum was valid.

An experienced Bitcoiner understands that this is not how secure entropy should be created. The ability to enter an existing mnemonic is necessary for restoring a wallet, and I am not presenting that fact as a unique vulnerability in one application.
But a beginner may not understand the distinction between:
“Enter an existing seed for recovery”
and:
“Choose twelve words to create a wallet.”

The BIP39 specification itself says the mnemonic is meant to transport computer-generated randomness, not human-created sentences. Yet an ordinary user can arrive at a valid-looking wallet while bringing weak human entropy into the system at the very first step.
The expert response is obvious:
You were not supposed to do that.
Exactly.
That is the point.

A secure system is not merely one that can be operated safely by someone who already knows every hidden rule. A good onboarding flow should make the safe path obvious and dangerous misunderstandings difficult.

In the Core model, the user does not need to invent the wallet’s root secret. Core generates the keys internally. The human-facing secret is the encryption passphrase, whose job is understandable: it unlocks an existing encrypted wallet.

That does not eliminate user responsibility. The passphrase must still be strong, backed up and kept separate. The computer must still be clean. The binaries should still be verified. The recovery must still be tested.
But the human is no longer invited to touch, transcribe and physically transport the root secret from which the wallet is derived.
That is not a cosmetic UX distinction.
It changes what the user is capable of accidentally exposing.

blocks.alt: We Made Bitcoin Self-Custody Harder Than It Had to Be — “You were not supposed to do that” is not a security model illustration
blocks.caption: Security includes what the interface invites a beginner to do, not only what an expert knows he should do.

blocks.html: The recovery phrase became a universal phishing API
Once an entire industry teaches users that recovery means entering a portable set of words, attackers receive a remarkably reusable script:
Your wallet is at risk. Enter your recovery words here.
The branding can change.
The fake application can imitate Trezor, Ledger, Coldcard or another wallet.
The message can arrive by email, text message, support ticket, search advertisement, telephone call or physical letter.
The supposed emergency can be a firmware problem, a database breach, an expiring wallet, an urgent migration, a replacement device or a mandatory security check.
The final instruction remains almost identical.
Enter the words.

Ledger’s 2020 e-commerce breach did not expose private keys, and it should never be described as though it did. It exposed something different: more than one million email addresses and approximately 272,000 detailed records containing names, telephone numbers, postal addresses and order information. That gave attackers a durable list of people who had purchased cryptocurrency-security devices and the language needed to target them convincingly. Later campaigns included extortion, fake support, physical letters and even an official-looking replacement device containing malicious instructions.

The same recovery ritual has been exploited through counterfeit applications. Users have reported losses after entering Trezor recovery phrases into fake applications distributed through official app stores. In April 2026, a counterfeit Ledger application in Apple’s App Store was linked through victim reports and on-chain tracing to at least $9.5 million in losses across more than fifty victims. The genuine hardware did not need to be broken. The attacker only needed the user to transfer the universally portable recovery secret into a counterfeit interface.
Other incidents belong to different failure classes.

The 2026 Coldcard incident was not BIP39 cryptography failing. Coinkite disclosed that affected firmware had generated seeds through a weaker-than-intended deterministic path, and public investigations linked the problem to active real-world theft. An independent strong passphrase could provide an additional barrier, and not every device, firmware version or wallet was affected. The narrower lesson is devastating enough:
A secure element can protect a weak key perfectly.
Air gaps, reputation and secure storage cannot compensate for failed key generation. Updating firmware may repair future generation, but it cannot make an already generated weak wallet stronger.
These incidents do not prove that every hardware wallet is unsafe.
They prove that self-custody is a lifecycle, not a chip.

The system includes entropy generation, firmware, build infrastructure, supply chains, companion applications, transaction construction, recovery, customer records, support channels, inheritance and the user’s own behavior. Protecting the key inside one component is valuable, but it does not make the rest of the system disappear.

The documented record is also not a complete census of every private loss or recovery mistake. That does not give us permission to invent incidents that have not been established. It does mean that public reports should be treated as evidence of known failure classes, not proof that all other failures have been reported.

blocks.alt: We Made Bitcoin Self-Custody Harder Than It Had to Be — The recovery phrase became a universal phishing API illustration
blocks.caption: Standardized recovery made wallets interoperable. It also standardized the instruction attackers need victims to follow.

blocks.html: Hardware isolation is real. It is not the whole wallet.
The strongest argument for a hardware wallet is real and should be stated honestly.
A properly designed hardware wallet can keep private keys isolated from ordinary malware running on an everyday computer.
That matters.
If the comparison is between a hardware wallet and a normal laptop used for browsing, email, downloading applications and opening random files, the hardware wallet has an obvious isolation advantage.
But that is not the comparison I am proposing.
I am comparing a hardware-wallet-centered system with a clean, dedicated generic computer running Linux and Bitcoin Core, kept permanently offline and used only to hold keys and sign PSBTs.
No browser.
No email.
No daily applications.
No connection to the Internet.
No cryptocurrency software ecosystem beyond Bitcoin Core.

That general-purpose computer contains more code and has its own firmware, hardware and supply-chain risks. Linux is not magic. An old ThinkPad is not blessed by cryptography. A badly administered generic computer may absolutely be worse than a well-designed hardware wallet.

The difference is that I can obtain the machine through the enormous ordinary computer market, wipe it, install verified software and repurpose it without creating a Bitcoin-specific customer record or relying on a small specialized signing-device vendor.

A hardware wallet may add a secure element and a smaller purpose-built interface, but the complete system can also add a manufacturer, shipping trail, reseller, authenticity procedure, firmware stack, firmware-signing infrastructure, update mechanism, companion application, support channel and highly recognizable recovery process.
Those are not automatically fatal dependencies.
They are dependencies that must be counted.

A hardware-wallet purchase can identify the customer as someone who probably owns portable digital assets before the device has generated a single key. The hardware wallet itself may be air-gapped. Its customer database, shipping provider and support platform are not.
For a small spending wallet, a phone or lightweight wallet may be entirely appropriate.

For meaningful long-term savings, my priority is different. I want the fewest unnecessary specialized assumptions I can reasonably achieve, and I want to understand the complete path from key generation to inheritance.
That is why “the private key never leaves the device” no longer ends the conversation for me.
The relevant question is whether the whole custody system preserves secrecy, transaction intent, availability and recoverability over its entire life.

blocks.html: Why Electrum made perfect sense in 2011
If the Core model is so coherent, why did so much of the industry move away from using Bitcoin Core as a wallet?
In my view, the largest practical reason is not wallet encryption or backup.
It is full validation.

Bitcoin Core asks the user to obtain and validate the chain. The initial synchronization takes time, bandwidth, processing and storage. Pruning can reduce the long-term storage requirement, but the blocks still need to be validated.
People wanted to start using Bitcoin immediately.

Electrum was created by Thomas Voegtlin in November 2011 and offered a brilliant answer to that problem. Its official description still calls the feature “Instant On”: Electrum is fast because it uses servers that index the Bitcoin blockchain, while the user keeps control of the private keys and verifies transaction history using SPV. Its early slogan captured the value proposition perfectly: the convenience of a web wallet without surrendering the keys to one.
The historical context matters.

In 2011 and 2012, the alternative for a normal user was not always a beautifully configured Bitcoin Core setup. Early custodial services were already showing how badly trusted convenience could fail. MyBitcoin disappeared in 2011 and later claimed a major loss, while Bitcoinica suffered repeated thefts in 2012 before shutting down.
Electrum solved a real problem.
It let the user keep the keys locally while obtaining the blockchain view from servers. It dramatically reduced the time between downloading a wallet and being ready to receive bitcoin.
I am not presenting that as a mistake.
It was a rational and valuable design trade-off.

But it also helped establish an expectation that self-custody should begin instantly. The user should not have to wait, validate the chain or think too deeply about the foundation before receiving an address.
Later hardware wallets and seed-based onboarding pushed that experience even further.
Unbox the device.
Write down the words.
Receive bitcoin.
Done.
That is excellent product onboarding.
It may not be the right philosophy for savings intended to remain secure for several decades.
There is also an important distinction that many people miss:
The offline Bitcoin Core signer does not need a synchronized blockchain to create keys, encrypt the wallet, restore a backup or sign a properly constructed PSBT.
The online machine needs the current chain state to identify spendable outputs, construct the transaction and broadcast it.
That means the full-node cost is paid by the online validation machine, not by every offline signer or every encrypted backup.
The architecture can be:
Online Bitcoin Core node constructs → offline Bitcoin Core wallet verifies and signs → online node broadcasts.
Once I understood that separation, the model became much less intimidating.

blocks.html: The real cost of Core is patience
I think of the initial synchronization like the foundation of a house.
The foundation is not the exciting part.
It takes time. It costs money. Nobody invites friends over to admire concrete while it cures.
But if the house is expected to remain standing for generations, we do not remove half the foundation because we want to use the kitchen this afternoon.
We take the time once because everything else rests on it.
That is increasingly how I see full validation.
For a spending wallet holding a small amount, convenience may deserve priority.
For long-term savings, the time horizon is different.

Bitcoin itself operates on a century-scale monetary schedule. If I am building a custody system intended to protect savings for ten, thirty or fifty years, and perhaps transfer responsibility to my family, spending additional hours or days establishing the foundation does not strike me as excessive.
It strikes me as proportionate.
This also changed how I think about inheritance.
For the first time, I feel that I can explain the basic recovery model to my own parents in language they already understand:
Here is the encrypted wallet backup.
Here is where the strong passphrase is preserved separately.
Here are the written recovery instructions.
You need the vault and the key.
Do not put them together.
Follow the restore procedure that we have already tested.
Inheritance will always involve communication, timing, people and some degree of trust. It is not the same problem as backup, and no file format removes the human part.
But “vault plus separately stored key” is a mental model I can explain.

“Here are twenty-four words, an optional passphrase that creates an entirely different wallet, a derivation convention, a script policy and a device-recovery ritual that may need to be reconstructed decades from now” is much harder.
This is why I am not convinced that Core is realistic only for technically sophisticated people.
The current interface is unfinished from a mainstream UX perspective, especially for watch-only construction, offline signing, descriptors, multisig and more complex Taproot policies.
That is a design problem.
It is not evidence that the underlying security architecture is too complicated.
The real opportunity for the next decade is not to keep making weaker mental models easier to sell.
It is to make the stronger architecture radically easier to use.

blocks.html: What I am actually recommending
I am not saying that every BIP39 setup is weak.

A knowledgeable user can generate strong entropy, use a strong independent passphrase, preserve the required wallet context, keep the components separate and test recovery. That can be a robust custody system.
I am saying that this is not how the dominant beginner story is usually presented.

The industry presents twelve or twenty-four human-readable words as the simple answer, then gradually adds steel, passphrases, multisig, vendor diversification, backup products, recovery services and increasingly elaborate ceremonies to manage the consequences of concentrating so much authority in one portable object.
At some point, it is reasonable to stop asking which product we should add next and ask whether the foundation was right.
My answer today is increasingly clear.
For meaningful long-term savings, I prefer:

generic hardware → clean dedicated Linux → Bitcoin Core → full validation → offline PSBT signing → strong wallet encryption → redundant encrypted wallet backups → separately stored passphrase → tested recovery
That is not a magic formula.
Bitcoin Core can contain bugs.
Linux can contain bugs.
A generic computer can be compromised.
A passphrase can be lost.
A backup can fail.
A user can still approve the wrong transaction.

The standard is not perfection. The standard is whether each added component removes more risk than it creates, whether I understand the complete system, and whether I can reproduce and test it without depending on a specialized Bitcoin product ecosystem.
Nobody should move meaningful savings into a new architecture merely because he read one article.
Start with a small amount.
Create the encrypted wallet.
Back it up.
Restore it on a clean system.
Verify the expected addresses.
Create a watch-only wallet.
Construct a PSBT.
Inspect the destination and fee on the offline signer.
Sign it.
Broadcast it.
Then repeat the procedure until it is boring.
Self-custody is not the purchase of a box.
It is a competence.

BIP39 made recovery portable, and that was a major contribution. But portability is not automatically security, human readability is not automatically safety, and interoperability is not the same thing as preserving the complete wallet.
We do not need a better way to hide the same plaintext root secret.
We need a better mental model.
The last decade taught people to treat the key as the vault.
The next decade should teach them to separate the two.
Back to first principles.
Back to the actual wallet.
Back to independent validation.
Back to Bitcoin Core.
